1	# A10 Project Purpose Contract — FROZEN 2026-11-17
2	
3	Date drafted: 2026-11-17. Analyst: Matt Sorensen. AI role: Problem Setter, then Challenger (Claude Code, decision-statement-builder skill).
4	Source candidate: #1 in `report/A10_problem_scan_2026-11-17.md`.
5	Status: **FROZEN 2026-11-17, approved by Matt Sorensen.** This was done before any analysis of how inputs relate to the outcome; only structural profiling and join tests have been run. Any later change requires a dated amendment, added below, with a stated reason.
6	
7	## Contract fields
8	
9	| Field | Contract answer |
10	|---|---|
11	| **Purpose pathway** | **Predictive** (the one primary path). An explanatory layer reports how much director track record adds to the prediction. That's association only, with no causal claim. |
12	| **Decision** | At the financing stage, before production, the acquisitions team decides for each incoming project whether to **flag for deep review**, **proceed on standard review**, or **pass**. |
13	| **Action** | Each year, the 20% of projects with the highest predicted risk go to deep review (comparable-film analysis, a second reader, renegotiating terms). The rest get standard review. The screen never rejects a project on its own. |
14	| **Decision time** | When the financing decision is made, before production. **Allowed inputs:** budget, genre, director's track record from earlier films only, production companies' track record from earlier films only, planned runtime, planned release month and quarter, original language, production country. **Prohibited inputs (known only after release):** revenue, box office, vote counts and averages, popularity, critic and audience scores, review text, TMDB keywords (crowd-edited after release). |
15	| **Population & unit** | Unit = **one feature film at its financing decision.** Population = feature films released 2000–2023 with a reported budget ≥ $1M and reported worldwide revenue > 0, excluding adult titles. Training: 2000–2015. Test: 2016–2019. Stress test: 2020–2023 (COVID era), reported separately. |
16	| **Outcome / target & horizon** | Positive class = **"money-loser": worldwide revenue < 2.5 × budget.** The 2.5× multiple is a labeled assumption (a commonly cited rule of thumb for covering marketing and the exhibitor's share). It's rerun at 1×, 2× and 3× as a sensitivity check. Horizon = full theatrical run as recorded in TMDB. The model estimates each project's probability of being a money-loser. |
17	| **Baseline** | (a) **Random 20% flagging**, which catches losers at the base rate (the floor). (b) **A simple rule:** flag projects in the genre × budget-tier groups with the highest historical loss rate, using training years only. The model has to beat (b), not just (a). |
18	| **Evidence standard** | On the 2016–2019 test films, the share of all money-losers that fall inside the flagged top 20% (capture rate). The model must beat rule (b) by **≥ 5 percentage points**, with a bootstrap 95% CI that excludes 0. Also report precision at 20%, calibration, and the result for the 2020–2023 stress set. *Bar confirmed by Matt at the freeze.* |
19	| **Value** | More money-losers reach deep review without adding review workload: same 20% capacity, better targeting. Value per year = (extra losers caught × loss avoided per caught loser × share of flagged deals actually changed) − (good films wrongly flagged × cost of a wrongly flagged deal). Each term is a **blank the owner fills in**; the report shows break-even values, not invented dollars. |
20	| **Constraints** | Review capacity: 20% of projects. Data rights: Kaggle public datasets, license recorded in the Data Receipt. Timing: frozen analysis by Nov 25, due Dec 4. No individual-level sensitive data, but director names are personal names, so results are reported at the aggregate or feature level, not as rankings of named people. Simplest adequate method: logistic regression first. |
21	| **Owner** | **Head of Acquisitions** at a representative film co-financier. This is a stand-in role: there are no real stakeholder interviews, and the report states that limitation. The owner is accountable for using the screen, monitoring it, and stopping it. |
22	
23	## Rival framing
24	**#2, director premium:** the greenlight committee decides whether to pay extra for a director with a strong track record. It uses the same data and time but asks a different question: what one input is worth, not sorting projects. It's the fallback if #1 fails the red-team or stop condition S1.
25	
26	## Prohibited uses
27	The screen must never quietly become:
28	1. **A tool for hiring or blacklisting people.** It must not rank, score or exclude individual directors or other talent, or feed into pay negotiations.
29	2. **An automatic reject.** A flag only sends a project to deep review, and a person makes the final call.
30	3. **A causal claim.** "Directors with strong track records *cause* profit" isn't supported. Track record is a predictive input and nothing more.
31	4. **A screen applied outside its population.** It doesn't cover micro-budget films (< $1M), streaming-only releases, or films without a theatrical revenue record.
32	
33	## Minimum evidence to move forward, and stop conditions
34	**Move to a pilot** (run alongside human review for one slate, with no decisions changed) only if S1 passes, calibration is acceptable on the test films, and capture on the 2020–2023 stress set doesn't fall below the rule baseline.
35	
36	| # | Stop trigger (observable) | Disposition |
37	|---|---|---|
38	| S1 | The model doesn't beat rule (b) by ≥ 5 pts of capture on 2016–2019 with a CI that excludes 0 | **Satisfice:** recommend the simple rule |
39	| S2 | Removing director track record changes capture by < 2 pts | Drop the director claim and report it as a null finding |
40	| S3 | The hand-check of 50 joined pairs shows > 10% wrong matches | Drop the RT join and use production-company track record as the focal factor |
41	| S4 | Films with a budget but no reported revenue are a large share of the population, and the cross-check with RT box office shows they skew toward losers | Restrict the claim to films with reported revenue, or **redirect** |
42	
43	## Red-team (Challenger)
44	
45	**Weakest link 1: a filter I set earlier selected on the outcome. *This is an AI correction.*** The "usable films" filter I used in the join tests required **≥ 50 TMDB votes**. Vote count is measured after release and rises with success (Spearman 0.48 with log ROI). Filtering on it silently drops obscure flops, which are exactly the films the screen exists to catch. That would make the loss rate look lower and the model look better than it is. **Fix:** the population now uses budget ≥ $1M and revenue > 0, with no vote filter (see above). This is a strong candidate for the report's required "material AI correction."
46	
47	**Weakest link 2: films with missing revenue.** 84,135 released TMDB films have a budget, but only 18,398 also have revenue. Films with no revenue on record are likely to include unreported flops. If so, the population is short on losers, and the base rate and capture will be biased. **Fix:** Phase 2 measures how many films have a budget ≥ $1M but no revenue, and uses RT domestic box office to estimate what those films earned (stop condition S4).
48	
49	**Weakest link 3: is the value logic real?** Real financiers have scripts, cast packages, comparable films and presale data that a public-data screen doesn't. So could this ever beat their judgment? **Answer:** it isn't meant to replace their judgment. It's a base-rate check that decides where scarce deep-review time goes. The value claim is limited to "better targeting at the same capacity," and the report must say that we can't compare against the experts' actual track record, which isn't in the data.
50	
51	**Weakest link 4: inputs that sit between "planned" and "actual."** TMDB records the *final* budget and runtime, not the planned ones, and they can drift during production, possibly more for troubled productions. That's a mild leak. **Fix:** report it as a limitation, and as a robustness check, refit using budget tiers rather than exact dollars.
52	
53	**Did the dataset pick this problem?** Partly, and the scan flags it. Budget and revenue being available made this candidate feasible. The decision (where to spend limited review time) is still real and has an owner, so it stays, with the population limits stated openly.
54

56	1. *Predicting, changing, or describing?* Predicting: the risk of a loss at the financing stage. The director layer describes only, and nothing here claims to change outcomes.
57	2. *Where's the evidence and data receipt?* TMDB and the two RT files in `data/raw/`. The Data Receipt is plan step 8, still to do.
58	3. *What would make us stop, and would we recognize it?* S1–S4 above. Each one is a number checked against a stated threshold.
59	4. *Which CRISP-DM phase are we in?* Business Understanding. Only structural profiling has been done; no relationships with the outcome have been modeled.
60	5. *What exact quantity is being claimed?* The share of 2016–2019 money-losers (revenue < 2.5× budget) caught in the top 20% of predicted risk, compared with the genre × budget rule, with a 95% CI.

## Claude  (2026-11-21T03:59:45.588Z)

I read the README (one line) and both A10 docs. Here's what we're working on.

## The project
This is the A10 team project for EMBA 560. It's due **Fri Dec 4, 2026 at 3:30 PM** and is worth 120 points. Matt Sorensen wrote both docs. I'm guessing you're the "one colleague" in the plan.

**The question:** Can a model built only on information available before production flag which film projects are likely to lose money, better than a simple rule can?

- **Decision owner:** a stand-in Head of Acquisitions at a film co-financier. For each project at the financing stage, they choose deep review, standard review or pass.
- **Action:** the riskiest 20% of projects get deep review. The screen never rejects a project on its own.
- **Target:** "money-loser" means worldwide revenue is less than 2.5× budget. The 2.5× is an assumption, so it gets rerun at 1×, 2× and 3×.
- **Population:** films released 2000–2023 with a budget of at least $1M and revenue above $0, excluding adult titles. There's **no vote-count filter**. That filter was removed as an AI correction because vote count is measured after release and leaks the outcome.
- **Split:** train on 2000–2015, test on 2016–2019, and run a separate stress test on 2020–2023 (the COVID years).
- **Allowed inputs:** budget, genre, runtime, release month and quarter, language, country, and the track records of the director and production companies from earlier films only. Anything measured after release is off-limits: revenue, votes, popularity, scores, reviews and keywords.
- **What counts as success:** logistic regression has to catch at least 5 percentage points more of the 2016–2019 money-losers in its top 20% than the genre × budget-tier rule does. That's called the capture rate. The bootstrap 95% CI also has to exclude 0.
- **Stop conditions:**
  - S1: the model misses that bar, so we recommend the simple rule instead.
  - S2: removing director track record changes capture by less than 2 points, so the director claim is reported as a null finding.
  - S3: more than 10% of the joined title pairs we hand-check are wrong matches, so we drop the RT join.
  - S4: films with a budget but no reported revenue skew toward losers, so the claim gets narrowed.
- **Data:** a TMDB dataset of 1.54M rows, plus Rotten Tomatoes (RT) reviews and movies files from Kaggle. The title+year join matched about 80% of films. The RT movies file also adds director names.

## Where the plan stands
- **Phase 0 (setup):** done. Splitting the work between you and Matt was deferred, and the plan treats Matt as owning everything for now.
- **Phase 1 (purpose contract):** done. The contract was frozen on Nov 17. Step 7 is still unchecked in the plan, but the contract file says it's frozen, so the checklist is just out of date.
- **Phase 2 (Data Receipt and data understanding, Nov 19–21):** should be underway, but nothing is checked off. This covers recording each source, profiling every field, verifying the join with a 50-pair hand-check, and the S4 check on missing revenue.
- **Phases 3–4 (preparation and modeling):** must be finished by **Nov 25**. The plan says that if work runs behind, the second model and the early-buzz feature get cut first.

## What's in this repo and what isn't
- There's only a README and these two docs.
- None of the folders from the plan are here: `data/raw`, `notebooks/`, `ai_logs/`, `report/`.
- The CSVs, the problem scan report and Matt's notebook aren't here either. The paths in the plan point to Matt's Windows machine.
- The plan also has some stale bits. Its "Direction" section still describes the old filter (budget ≥ $100K and at least 50 votes, about 7,716 films), which the frozen contract replaced.

**What's your role, and what do you want to tackle first?** Some options:
1. Set up the folder layout here and pull in the data.
2. Start Phase 2 work (Data Receipt, profiling, verifying the join).
3. Do an independent rebuild as your own track. Appendix D asks for an independent rebuild of 3–5 key numbers.

Also, are the data files somewhere I can get to, or do they need to be downloaded from Kaggle?

I created both notebooks, and your notebook ran from start to finish with no errors.

- **`notebooks/A10-master.ipynb`** has only a title cell. It's where the final shared work will be merged from both your notebooks.
- **`notebooks/Edwards-A10.ipynb`** has the imports and loads all five files. It profiles every column (type, % missing, distinct values) and checks Matt's numbers. It only describes the data's structure: the contract says not to look at how inputs relate to the outcome until features are built.

## Matt's numbers check out
| Check | Matt's figure | Mine |
|---|---|---|
| Released films with budget > 0 | 84,135 | **84,135** ✓ |
| …that also have revenue > 0 | 18,398 | **18,398** ✓ |
| RT movies rows / duplicate ids | 143,258 / 1,206 | **143,258 / 1,206** ✓ |
| RT reviews rows / distinct movies | ~1.44M / ~69k | 1,444,963 / 69,263 ✓ |

So the head start is solid on these numbers.

## Three new findings
1. **S4 may be triggered.** The contract population is **5,766 films**. Another **4,455 films** have a budget of at least $1M but no revenue on record, which is 44% of all films with that budget. Stop condition S4 kicks in when this group is "a large share" *and* it skews toward money-losers. The first half looks met. The second half needs the cross-check against RT box office. That should be the next validation, because a failure means narrowing the claim or redirecting the project.
2. **TMDB has 1,407 duplicate film ids.** The plan doesn't mention them. They need a line in the cleaning ledger, and I haven't checked yet how many are inside the population.
3. **The test set is small.** It's 1,086 films from 2016–2019, so the top 20% is about 217 flagged films. The bootstrap confidence interval will be wide, which makes the ≥5-point bar hard to clear. That's worth knowing now, not on Nov 25.

The notebook also flags 34,165 placeholder budgets under $1,000 and 374K missing release dates. Those go in the cleaning ledger later.

Nothing is committed yet. The notebook has outputs saved locally, and `nbstripout` will strip them when you commit. **Should I commit the repo setup and both notebooks?** After that, I'd do the S4 check next.

I've **added** the Box Office Mojo file rather than replacing anything. It's in `get_data.py`, the README's data sources table and your notebook, and the notebook still runs from start to finish.

**Why it can't replace anything:** it only has **domestic (US) grosses**. The contract's target is worldwide revenue against budget, so TMDB stays the core source. What this file *can* do is give an independent check on revenue, alongside the RT `boxOffice` column. It has two advantages there: daily data with dates, and coverage from 2000 to Jan 2025.

**What I found:**
- 356K rows, one per film per day, covering **7,176 titles**.
- The `id` column is unique for **every row**, so it can't be used as a film key. The only way to join is on title + year.
- A quick title + year (±1) match links **59% of the contract population** (3,387 of 5,766 films).
- **Early S4 signal:** only **4%** of the 4,455 films with a budget but no revenue (187 films) show up in Box Office Mojo at all. That suggests most of them never had a tracked US theatrical release, rather than being hidden flops. If that holds up, many of them are outside the population anyway (prohibited use #4 excludes films with no theatrical revenue record). That's good news for S4. But this was a rough match with no hand-check, so treat it as a lead, not a finding.

**For the Data Receipt:** the data was scraped from Box Office Mojo, which IMDb owns, and published through a personal GitHub repo. It has no Kaggle-style license, so the report should say that.

## Claude  (2026-11-21T04:43:43.078Z)

I checked this before recommending anything. TMDB's financial data is missing **unevenly**, and that matters more than how much is missing.

**TMDB coverage for the 5,866 US theatrical releases (2000–2023) I could match** (86% of Box Office Mojo's titles):

| Domestic gross | Films | Has budget | Has budget + revenue |
|---|---|---|---|
| under $1M | 2,077 | 26% | **18%** |
| $1–10M | 1,064 | 61% | 56% |
| $10–50M | 1,491 | 90% | 87% |
| $50M+ | 1,234 | 98% | 97% |

So TMDB covers films that did well and is missing the small films that flopped. Those are the money-losers the screen is supposed to catch. This is S4's worry, now with evidence: the population as defined has too few losers.

**Switching to US domestic only doesn't fix this.** The bottleneck is **budget**, not revenue. A money-loser is defined by revenue relative to budget, and neither Box Office Mojo nor RT has budgets. With domestic-only data we'd still get budgets from TMDB, with the same gap. We'd also lose the worldwide revenue that the 2.5× rule is based on.

**Realistic options:**
1. **Find a better budget source.** The Numbers (the-numbers.com) is the industry-standard public budget list, about 6,000 films, with domestic and worldwide grosses, and Kaggle has scraped copies. It probably shares the same bias (studios disclose budgets for bigger films), but it would fill some gaps and gives an independent check on TMDB's figures.
2. **Narrow the claim.** S4 already plans for this: "restrict the claim to films with reported revenue." The screen would cover films with disclosed budgets, and the report would use the Box Office Mojo table above to show exactly how that population is skewed. It would need a dated amendment to the frozen contract.
3. **Change the target to something that doesn't need budget**, for example "domestic gross under $X." That changes the decision itself, which is close to starting over 13 days before the deadline.

**My recommendation: option 1 to see how much it helps, then option 2 for whatever gap is left.** Either way, the coverage table above is strong material for the report. It turns S4 from a guess into a measured finding.

Do you want me to look for a The Numbers dataset on Kaggle, or do you already have one in mind? Also, because this touches the frozen contract, you'll probably want Matt's agreement before any amendment. I haven't changed anything yet.

I found several Kaggle datasets built from The Numbers that include production budget and worldwide gross, though none was clearly the official one.

- **Top 500 Movies by Production Budget** (mitchellharrison): The top 500 films by production budget as judged by The Numbers. Production budgets are not inflation adjusted, and the creator notes that budget and box office figures are hard to pin down.
- **Top 4000 Movies - Exploratory Data Analysis** (danielodonoghue15): A notebook with a CSV of the top 4000 movies by production budget according to The Numbers website. It includes release date, title, budget, and gross. The creator warns the money figures are not adjusted for inflation, and are also not likely to be very exact.
- **Movies Metrics, Features and Statistics** (michaelmatta0): Covers 6.5K top movies worldwide of all time, scraped from The Numbers. Its fields include production budget and worldwide gross.
- **The Ultimate Film Statistics Dataset** (alessandrolobello): Combines data from Wikipedia, The Numbers, and IMDb, with production budgets and worldwide gross earnings.

The other results were not built from The Numbers. They included a 2000–2024 box office set, a 2024–2026 set sourced from Wikipedia-style fields, and several synthetic datasets. ## Claude  (2026-11-21T04:47:58.079Z)

I've looked at what The Numbers data provides. The short answer: **it doesn't fix the gap, but it's still useful.**

**The best version:** [michaelmatta0 / Movies Metrics, Features and Statistics](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/michaelmatta0/movies-ultimate-metrics-features-and-metadata), scraped from The Numbers.
- 6,569 films, **4,936 from 2000–2023**.
- Production budget, domestic / international / worldwide gross, opening weekend, video sales.
- Columns that would be known before release: production/financing companies (36% missing), MPAA rating, source material (e.g. book adaptation), creative type, franchise, genre, runtime, countries and languages.
- Data quality issues: some dates go up to 2068, the smallest budget is $86, and 422 films have $0 worldwide gross.

I also checked [alessandrolobello / Ultimate Film Statistics](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/alessandrolobello/the-ultimate-film-statistics-dataset-for-ml). It's smaller (4,380 films), and most of its columns are IMDb ratings measured after release, so I'd skip it.

**Coverage of all 6,806 US theatrical releases from 2000–2023:**

| Domestic gross | Films | TMDB has budget + revenue | The Numbers | Either |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| under $1M | 2,764 | 14% | 10% | **18%** |
| $1–10M | 1,223 | 49% | 45% | 60% |
| $10–50M | 1,549 | 84% | 83% | 91% |
| $50M+ | 1,270 | 94% | 92% | 97% |
| **All** | | 51% | 48% | **57%** |

(These percentages are lower than the table I showed earlier. That table only counted films that matched a TMDB row; this one counts every Box Office Mojo title.)

**What this tells us:**
1. **The gap is structural, not a TMDB problem.** Small films rarely make their budgets public anywhere. The Numbers has the same bias, and combining the two sources only moves the under-$1M tier from 14% to 18%. No free dataset will fix that. So the narrowed claim (option 2, an amendment saying "films with disclosed budgets") is probably unavoidable, and the coverage table becomes evidence for it in the report.
2. **The Numbers is a good validation source.** It lets us check TMDB's budget and revenue figures against an independent source, film by film, which is the kind of validation you mentioned wanting.
3. **It may be a better feature source than TMDB.** Production companies, MPAA rating, source material, franchise and creative type are all known at financing time, and none of them are in TMDB.

Nothing has been added to `data/raw` or `get_data.py` yet. The files are only in the kagglehub cache. For the Data Receipt: it was scraped from the-numbers.com (owned by Nash Information Services), so like Box Office Mojo it has no clean license.

**How do you want to proceed?**
- **(a)** Add The Numbers as a validation and feature source next to TMDB, and drop Box Office Mojo unless we use it for the coverage evidence.
- **(b)** Use The Numbers as the core financial source and TMDB as backup.
- **(c)** Something else.

I'd recommend (a). TMDB's coverage is slightly higher, and keeping it core means less to change in Matt's frozen setup.

Sources:
- [Movies Metrics, Features and Statistics (michaelmatta0)](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/michaelmatta0/movies-ultimate-metrics-features-and-metadata)
- [The Ultimate Film Statistics Dataset (alessandrolobello)](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/alessandrolobello/the-ultimate-film-statistics-dataset-for-ml)

## Claude  (2026-11-22T06:16:50.387Z)

No objection to searching, but the 1M rows are the wrong baseline. Most TMDB rows are shorts, TV movies, direct-to-video, or films budgeted under $1M, and those are outside the contract population whether or not they have financials. The real ceiling is **films that had a theatrical release**: Box Office Mojo lists about 6,800 US theatrical releases from 2000–2023, and we already have 6,755 usable films. So we probably have about a third to a half of the films that could ever qualify.

That said, the one big public source we haven't tried is **Wikidata** (Wikipedia's structured data, which has budgets and box office). I'll check how much it has.

## Claude  (2026-11-22T06:18:34.855Z)

You're right to check, and I did. Each extra source adds less than the one before:

| Added source | New usable films |
|---|---|
| The Numbers | +989 (+17%) |
| Wikidata (budget and box office in USD), on top of that | **+202 (+3%)** |

The other sources mostly repeat what TMDB already has, because they all draw on the same studio-reported figures. The missing 95% of TMDB is mostly films that never needed or published a budget: shorts, TV, direct-to-video, micro-budget.

**About 7,000 films is still workable** for logistic regression with a handful of inputs. The real constraint is the 2016–2019 test set, which grows from about 1,100 to about 1,300 films.

My recommendation: use TMDB + The Numbers, and optionally Wikidata, and stop searching. Agree?

Title + year matcher\n\n1. **Normalize titles:** strip accents, lowercase, `&` → `and`, drop a leading *The / A / An*, keep letters and digits only.\n2. **Candidates:** same normalized title as TMDB's `title` **or** `original_title`, release year within ±2.\n3. **Pick the best candidate** per source film: budget agrees (±15%), then closest year, then closest runtime, then most TMDB votes (votes only break ties for identity; they're never a model input).\n4. **Year differences need corroboration:** if years differ, runtime must be within 10 minutes or the budget must agree.\n5. **One-to-one only:** a TMDB film claimed by two source films is dropped from both.\"\"\"),\ncode(\"\"\"def norm_title(s: pd.Series) -> pd.Series:\n    s = s.fillna(\"\").astype(str).map(lambda x: unicodedata.normalize(\"NFKD\", x).encode(\"ascii\", \"ignore\").decode())\n    s = s.str.lower().str.replace(\"&\", \" and \", regex=False)\n    s = s.str.replace(r\"^(the|a|an)\\\\s+\", \"\", regex=True)\n    return s.str.replace(r\"[^a-z0-9]\", \"\", regex=True)\n\n\ntmdb_keys = pd.concat([\n    tmdb.assign(key=norm_title(tmdb[\"title\"])),\n    tmdb.assign(key=norm_title(tmdb[\"original_title\"])),\n]).drop_duplicates([\"id\", \"key\"])\ntmdb_keys = tmdb_keys.loc[tmdb_keys[\"key\"].ne(\"\"), [\"id\", \"key\", \"year\", \"runtime\", \"budget\", \"vote_count\"]]\n\n\ndef match_to_tmdb(src, title_col, runtime_col=None, budget_col=None, name=\"src\"):\n    \\\"\\\"\\\"Return src_row -> TMDB id, one-to-one, with match diagnostics.\\\"\\\"\\\"\n    s = pd.DataFrame({\"src_row\": np.arange(len(src)), \"key\": norm_title(src[title_col]), \"src_year\": src[\"year\"]})\n    s[\"src_runtime\"] = src[runtime_col] if runtime_col else np.nan\n    s[\"src_budget\"] = src[budget_col] if budget_col else np.nan\n    m = s.merge(tmdb_keys, on=\"key\")\n    m[\"year_diff\"] = (m[\"src_year\"] - m[\"year\"]).abs()\n    m = m[m[\"year_diff\"] <= 2]\n    m[\"runtime_diff\"] = (m[\"src_runtime\"] - m[\"runtime\"]).abs()\n    m[\"budget_agrees\"] = m[\"budget\"].gt(0) & ((m[\"budget\"] / m[\"src_budget\"] - ##### [45] markdown
## 4. Build and verify the TMDB-RT join (plan step 10)

**Why join at all:** TMDB has no director field. The focal factor (director track record) comes from RT's `director`, and the S4 missing-revenue check needs RT's `boxOffice`. Neither file shares an id with the other, so films are matched on **title, release year (±1) and runtime**.

**Rules, fixed before looking at the results:**
1. Titles are normalized: accents removed, lower case, `&` → `and`, punctuation dropped, spaces collapsed.
2. A candidate pair needs the same normalized title (TMDB `title`, or `original_title` as a fallback) and an RT year within ±1 of the TMDB year. The RT year is the theatrical date's year, or the streaming date's year when there's no theatrical date.
   - **2b (added 2026-11-18, after the first pass):** an RT record with **only a streaming date** may have a streaming year later than TMDB year + 1, **if the runtimes agree within 5 minutes.** *Why:* the first pass left 447 films unmatched whose title was in RT. Most were international films whose only RT date is a streaming date 2–10 years after release (e.g., "English Vinglish," 2012 release, 2016 RT streaming date, 134 vs. 133 minutes). The runtime check replaces the year as the second piece of evidence. This rule was set by looking at match quality, never at the outcome.
3. If a film has several candidates, a title match beats an `original_title` match, rule 2 beats rule 2b, then the closest year wins, then the closest runtime.
4. **One-to-one:** if one RT record is the best match for two TMDB films, both pairs are dropped as ambiguous rather than guessed.
5. **Verification:** a random sample of 50 matched pairs is checked by hand, plus 10 extra pairs drawn only from rule 2b (a random 50 would include just 2 or 3 of them). Stop condition S3 is judged on the random 50: more than 10% wrong matches drops the RT join, and production-company track record becomes the focal factor. If 2 or more of the 10 rule-2b pairs are wrong, rule 2b is dropped.

This section writes two files to `../data/clean/`: the crosswalk (TMDB id ↔ RT id) and the hand-check sheet. The hand-check sheet is written **once** and never overwritten, because Matt fills it in by hand.

import re
import unicodedata

def norm_title(s):
    s = s.fillna("").astype(str).map(
        lambda x: unicodedata.normalize("NFKD", x).encode("ascii", "ignore").decode())
    s = s.str.lower().str.replace("&", " and ", regex=False)
    s = s.str.replace(r"[^a-z0-9 ]", " ", regex=True)
    return s.str.replace(r"\s+", " ", regex=True).str.strip()

# RT side: one row per RT id (2c: 1,206 repeated ids, all but 2 exact copies; keep the first)

rt_theat = pd.to_datetime(rtj["releaseDateTheaters"], errors="coerce").dt.year
rt_stream = pd.to_datetime(rtj["releaseDateStreaming"], errors="coerce").dt.year
rtj["rt_year"] = rt_theat.fillna(rt_stream)
rtj["rt_year_source"] = np.where(rt_theat.notna(), "theatrical", np.where(rt_stream.notna(), "streaming", "none"))
rtj["key"] = norm_title(rtj["title"])
rtj = rtj[rtj["key"].ne("") & rtj["rt_year"].notna()]

# TMDB side: the contract population
tj = pop[["id", "title", "original_title", "year", "runtime", "budget", "revenue", "period"]].copy()
tj["key_title"] = norm_title(tj["title"])
tj["key_orig"] = norm_title(tj["original_title"])

print(f"RT records usable for matching: {len(rtj):,} of {rt_movies['id'].nunique():,} unique ids "
      f"(year source: {rtj['rt_year_source'].value_counts().to_dict()})")
print(f"TMDB films to match: {len(tj):,}")

# Candidate pairs: same normalized title (title first, original_title as fallback), year within +/-1
rt_cols = ["id", "key", "title", "rt_year", "rt_year_source", "runtimeMinutes", "director", "boxOffice"]
rt_side = rtj[rt_cols].rename(columns={"id": "rt_id", "title": "rt_title"})
cands = []
for key_col, how in [("key_title", "title"), ("key_orig", "original_title")]:
    c = tj.merge(rt_side, left_on=key_col, right_on="key", how="inner")
    c["matched_on"] = how
    cands.append(c)
cands = pd.concat(cands, ignore_index=True)
signed = cands["rt_year"] - cands["year"]
cands["year_diff"] = signed.abs()
cands["runtime_diff"] = (cands["runtimeMinutes"] - cands["runtime"].replace(0, np.nan)).abs()
rule2 = cands["year_diff"] <= 1
rule2b = (cands["rt_year_source"] == "streaming") & (signed > 1) & (cands["runtime_diff"] <= 5)
cands["rule"] = np.where(rule2, "2: year +/-1", np.where(rule2b, "2b: later streaming + runtime", None))
cands = cands[rule2 | rule2b].copy()

# Best candidate per TMDB film: title before original_title, rule 2 before 2b, closest year, closest runtime
cands["title_rank"] = cands["matched_on"].map({"title": 0, "original_title": 1})
cands["rule_rank"] = cands["rule"].str.startswith("2b").astype(int)
cands = cands.sort_values(["id", "title_rank", "rule_rank", "year_diff", "runtime_diff"], na_position="last")
n_cands = cands.groupby("id")["rt_id"].nunique()
best = cands.drop_duplicates("id").copy()
best["n_candidates"] = best["id"].map(n_cands)

# One-to-one: an RT record claimed by two TMDB films is ambiguous; drop both
claimed = best["rt_id"].duplicated(keep=False)
ambiguous = best[claimed]
xwalk = best[~claimed].copy()

summary = pd.Series({
    "TMDB films in population": len(tj),
    "films with >= 1 candidate": best["id"].nunique(),
    "dropped: RT record claimed twice": ambiguous["id"].nunique(),
    "matched 1:1": len(xwalk),
    "  of which by rule 2b (later streaming + runtime)": int(xwalk["rule"].str.startswith("2b").sum()),
    "  of which matched on original_title": int((xwalk["matched_on"] == "original_title").sum()),
    "  of which had > 1 candidate": int((xwalk["n_candidates"] > 1).sum()),
    "unmatched": len(tj) - len(xwalk),
}, name="films")
display(summary.to_frame())
print(f"Match rate: {len(xwalk) / len(tj):.1%}")

A join that matches big films more often than small ones would bias everything built on it, including the director track record. So the match rate is checked by period and by budget tier. Unmatched films are split into "title not found in RT" and "title found, but the year is outside ±1".

### 4b. Do the matched pairs agree?
If the pairs are the same film, the two sources should agree on year and runtime, and RT's domestic box office should track TMDB's worldwide revenue. RT box office is domestic (US) only, so it's expected to be **lower** than TMDB's worldwide figure. A matched pair where RT is clearly *higher* points to a wrong match or a bad TMDB revenue.

### 4c. Save the crosswalk and the hand-check sheet
The crosswalk is rebuilt on every run. The hand-check sheet holds a random sample of 50 matched pairs plus 10 extra rule-2b pairs (seed 560); the `sample` column says which is which. It is written only if it doesn't exist yet, so Matt's answers are never overwritten. Each row has links to both websites.

**How to fill it in:** open `data/clean/join_handcheck.csv` in Excel. For each row, compare the two titles, years, runtimes and the RT director, and use the links if unsure. Put **Y** (same film) or **N** (different film) in `correct`, and add a short `note` for any N. Save as CSV.

### 4d. Hand-check result (stop condition S3)
Reads Matt's completed sheet. With only 50 pairs, the error rate is uncertain, so it's reported with a 95% Wilson interval next to the 10% threshold.
##### [55] code
hc = pd.read_csv(HANDCHECK, dtype={"correct": str, "note": str})
hc["answer"] = hc["correct"].fillna("").str.strip().str.upper()
if not hc["answer"].isin(["Y", "N"]).all():
    print(f"Hand-check pending: {hc['answer'].isin(['Y', 'N']).sum()} of {len(hc)} rows answered. "
          f"Fill in {HANDCHECK.name}, then rerun.")
else:
    def wilson(k, n, z=1.96):
        p = k / n
        centre = (p + z**2 / (2 * n)) / (1 + z**2 / n)
        half = z * np.sqrt(p * (1 - p) / n + z**2 / (4 * n**2)) / (1 + z**2 / n)
        return p, max(0, centre - half), centre + half

    r50 = hc[hc["sample"] == "random 50"]
    k = int(r50["answer"].eq("N").sum())
    p, lo, hi = wilson(k, len(r50))
    print(f"Random 50: {k} wrong = {p:.0%} (95% Wilson CI {lo:.0%} to {hi:.0%})")
    print("S3 (> 10% wrong):", "TRIGGERED: drop the RT join" if p > 0.10 else "not triggered: keep the RT join")
    b = hc[hc["rule"].str.startswith("2b")]
    kb = int(b["answer"].eq("N").sum())
    print(f"Rule 2b pairs checked (extra 10 + any in the random 50): {kb} wrong of {len(b)} -> "
          + ("drop rule 2b" if kb >= 2 else "keep rule 2b"))
    if hc["answer"].eq("N").any():
        display(hc[hc["answer"].eq("N")])
##### [56] markdown
### 4e. Join findings and verdict (hand-check by Matt Sorensen, 2026-11-19)

1. **Coverage:** 4,673 of 5,766 films (81.0%) matched one-to-one. 241 of them came through rule 2b. 14 films were dropped as ambiguous rather than guessed.
2. **Accuracy (stop condition S3):** Matt checked 60 pairs by hand: the random 50 and 10 extra rule-2b pairs. **0 of the random 50 were wrong (0%, 95% Wilson CI 0% to 7%).** Even the top of that interval is under the 10% threshold, so **S3 is not triggered: the RT join stays, and director track record stays the focal factor.** Rule 2b: 0 wrong of 11 checked, so it stays.
3. **Agreement:** 79% of pairs have the same year and 93% have runtimes within 5 minutes. RT domestic box office tracks TMDB revenue closely (Spearman 0.898, median ratio 0.50, as expected for domestic vs. worldwide).
4. **Coverage isn't even.** 58% of $1–5M films match, against 91% of $60M+ films, and the 2020–23 stress films match at 70.5%. Matched films are losers slightly less often than unmatched films (63.7% vs. 68.3%). Director track record will therefore be missing more often for small films and losers, so Phase 3 needs a "director unknown" indicator, not a dropped row.
5. **New label risk:** for 396 matched films (10.3%), TMDB "worldwide" revenue equals RT *domestic* box office within 2%. 87% of them are labelled losers, against 57% of the rest. Their foreign earnings are probably missing, which would make some false losers. This joins the revenue repairs (3k rows 1–2) and goes to the step 12 readiness gate.

**Outputs:** `data/clean/tmdb_rt_crosswalk.csv` (4,673 pairs, rebuilt each run) and `data/clean/join_handcheck.csv` (Matt's 60 answers; never overwritten).

##### [8]
def norm_title(s: pd.Series) -> pd.Series:
    s = s.fillna("").astype(str).map(lambda x: unicodedata.normalize("NFKD", x).encode("ascii", "ignore").decode())
    s = s.str.lower().str.replace("&", " and ", regex=False)
    s = s.str.replace(r"^(the|a|an)\s+", "", regex=True)
    return s.str.replace(r"[^a-z0-9]", "", regex=True)


tmdb_keys = pd.concat([
    tmdb.assign(key=norm_title(tmdb["title"])),
    tmdb.assign(key=norm_title(tmdb["original_title"])),
]).drop_duplicates(["id", "key"])
tmdb_keys = tmdb_keys.loc[tmdb_keys["key"].ne(""), ["id", "key", "year", "runtime", "budget", "vote_count"]]


def match_to_tmdb(src, title_col, runtime_col=None, budget_col=None, name="src"):
    """Return src_row -> TMDB id, one-to-one, with match diagnostics."""
    s = pd.DataFrame({"src_row": np.arange(len(src)), "key": norm_title(src[title_col]), "src_year": src["year"]})
    s["src_runtime"] = src[runtime_col] if runtime_col else np.nan
    s["src_budget"] = src[budget_col] if budget_col else np.nan
    m = s.merge(tmdb_keys, on="key")
    m["year_diff"] = (m["src_year"] - m["year"]).abs()
    m = m[m["year_diff"] <= 2]
    m["runtime_diff"] = (m["src_runtime"] - m["runtime"]).abs()
    m["budget_agrees"] = m["budget"].gt(0) & ((m["budget"] / m["src_budget"] - 1).abs() < 0.15)
    m = (m.sort_values(["src_row", "budget_agrees", "year_diff", "runtime_diff", "vote_count"],
                       ascending=[True, False, True, True, False], na_position="last")
          .drop_duplicates("src_row"))
    m = m[m["year_diff"].eq(0) | m["runtime_diff"].le(10) | m["budget_agrees"]]
    m = m[~m["id"].duplicated(keep=False)]
    print(f"{name:<12} matched {len(m):,} of {len(src):,} ({len(m) / len(src):.0%}); "
          f"year diff counts {m['year_diff'].value_counts().sort_index().to_dict()}")
    return m[["src_row", "id", "year_diff", "runtime_diff", "budget_agrees"]]


tn_match = match_to_tmdb(tn, "Movie Name", "Running Time (minutes)", "Production Budget (USD)", "The Numbers")
bom_match = match_to_tmdb(bom, "title", name="Box Office Mojo")
sl_match = match_to_tmdb(sl, "movie_title", "runtime", name="RT sl")

both = tn_match.merge(tmdb[["id", "budget"]], on="id")
both = both[both["budget"].gt(0)]
print(f"\nCheck: where TMDB and The Numbers both have a budget, they agree (±15%) for "
      f"{both['budget_agrees'].mean():.0%} of {len(both):,} matched films")
[9] md: ## 5. Attach the sources to TMDB
##### [10]
def attach(base, src, match, prefix, cols):
    part = src.iloc[match["src_row"]][cols].set_axis(match["id"].values)
    part.columns = [f"{prefix}_{c}" for c in cols]
    part[f"{prefix}_year_diff"] = match["year_diff"].values
    return base.merge(part, left_on="id", right_index=True, how="left")


tn_cols = ["Movie Name", "Release Date", "Production Budget (USD)", "Worldwide Gross (USD)", "Domestic Gross (USD)",
           "MPAA Rating", "Source", "Creative Type", "Production Method", "Franchise",
           "Production/Financing Companies", "Running Time (minutes)", "Movie URL"]
films = tmdb.copy()
films = attach(films, tn, tn_match, "tn", tn_cols)
films = attach(films, bom, bom_match, "bom", ["title", "first_date", "domestic_gross", "max_theaters"])
films = attach(films, sl, sl_match, "sl", ["rotten_tomatoes_link", "movie_title", "actors", "production_company", "directors"])
films = films.merge(wd.add_prefix("wd_").rename(columns={"wd_id": "id"}), on="id", how="left")
assert films["id"].is_unique

tn_new = tn.drop(index=tn_match["src_row"])

# Duplicate guard: same normalized title as a TMDB film with financials, year within +/-1
has_fin = films["year"].between(*YEARS) & (films["fin_budget"].notna() | films["fin_revenue"].notna())
tk = films.loc[has_fin, ["title", "original_title", "year"]]
tmdb_titles = pd.concat([pd.DataFrame({"key": norm_title(tk[c]), "y": tk["year"]}) for c in ["title", "original_title"]])
probe = pd.DataFrame({"key": norm_title(tn_new["Movie Name"]), "y": tn_new["year"]}, index=tn_new.index)
hits = probe.reset_index().merge(tmdb_titles, on="key", suffixes=("", "_t"))
dup_idx = hits.loc[(hits["y"] - hits["y_t"]).abs() <= 1, "index"].unique()
print(f"Not added (probable duplicates of TMDB films): {len(dup_idx)}")
tn_new = tn_new.drop(index=dup_idx).reset_index(drop=True)
rows = tn_new[tn_cols].add_prefix("tn_")
rows.insert(0, "id", -(np.arange(len(tn_new)) + 1))
rows["title"] = tn_new["Movie Name"].values
rows["original_title"] = tn_new["Movie Name"].values
rows["release_dt"] = pd.to_datetime(tn_new["Release Date"], errors="coerce").values
rows["year"] = tn_new["year"].values
rows["runtime"] = tn_new["Running Time (minutes)"].values
rows["tn_year_diff"] = 0
rows["fin_budget"] = rows["tn_Production Budget (USD)"].where(rows["tn_Production Budget (USD)"] > 0)
rows["fin_revenue"] = rows["tn_Worldwide Gross (USD)"].where(rows["tn_Worldwide Gross (USD)"] > 0)
rows["fin_budget_src"] = rows["fin_budget"].notna().map({True: "the_numbers", False: pd.NA})
rows["fin_revenue_src"] = rows["fin_revenue"].notna().map({True: "the_numbers", False: pd.NA})
rows["usable"] = rows["year"].between(*YEARS) & rows["fin_budget"].ge(BUDGET_FLOOR) & rows["fin_revenue"].gt(0)
rows["in_tmdb"] = False

films["in_tmdb"] = True
before = films["usable"].sum()
films = pd.concat([films, rows], ignore_index=True)
assert films["id"].is_unique
print(f"Added {len(rows):,} The Numbers-only films ({rows['usable'].sum():,} usable). "
      f"Usable films: {before:,} -> {films['usable'].sum():,}")

Late installments may show fatigue.\n- **Possible representation:**\n  - `is_sequel` (bool): installment number > 1\n  - `installment_number` (int): 1, 2, 3, …\n  - `in_franchise` (bool) and `franchise_name` (category): wider universe, e.g. MCU\n  - `prior_installments` (int): earlier films in the series/franchise released before this one\n  - Possibly: the previous installment's performance (multiple of budget), which is known before production\n- **Data sources:**\n  - The Numbers `tn_Franchise` (already in the unified file; sparse)\n  - Wikidata \"part of the series\" (P179), \"series ordinal\" (P1545), \"follows\" (P155). 188	2. **The grain is not clean in any file.**
189	   - TMDB: 1,060 ids appear more than once, and 1,019 of them have *conflicting* values across copies. Phase 3 needs an explicit rule for which copy to keep.
190	   - RT movies: 1,206 repeated slugs, almost all exact copies.
191	   - RT reviews: 24,788 rows share a reviewId, and 12,394 are exact duplicates.
192	3. **TMDB stores unknown values as 0, not blank.** Budget is unknown for 94.1% of all titles and revenue for 98.3%. The column-level missing table makes the data look complete, and it isn't.
193	4. **There are placeholder and future dates.** 1800-01-01 appears as a placeholder (2,217 TMDB titles, 71 RT reviews). 1,740 TMDB titles carry dates after the access date, meaning unreleased films. The population filter removes both.
194	5. **Budget entry errors.** 34,106 released films list a budget of $1–$999, which is almost certainly typed in millions or just junk. The $1M floor drops them, and that's an information loss to log in Phase 3.
195	6. **Population size (frozen contract):** 5,766 films. That's 4,145 for training (2000–2015), 1,086 for testing (2016–2019) and 535 for the stress test (2020–2023).
196	
197	**Material risk: missing revenue (stop condition S4)**
198	43.6% of films with a budget of at least $1M have **no revenue recorded** (41.7% train, 42.7% test, 55.9% stress). If those films are mostly flops that nobody bothered to report, the population is short on exactly the money-losers the screen exists to catch, and both the base rate and capture will be biased. That's checked in step 10, using RT domestic box office for the films that join.
199	
200	**Fitness disposition: FIT WITH CONDITIONS.** The sources support the contract's decision, unit and time order. The financial fields are volunteer-entered and need cleaning rules (duplicates, zeros, unit errors). The disposition becomes final only after the S4 check: if the films missing revenue turn out to skew toward losers, the claim is restricted to films with reported revenue, or the project redirects.

244	def numeric_profile(df, cols, zero_as_missing=()):
245	    # Center, spread and shape for each numeric column (Ch 6, Table 6.1)
246	    rows = []
247	    for c in cols:
248	        s = df[c].astype(float)
249	        if c in zero_as_missing:
250	            s = s.mask(s == 0)
251	        x = s.dropna()
252	        q1, q3 = x.quantile([0.25, 0.75])
253	        iqr = q3 - q1
254	        rows.append({
255	            "field": c, "n": len(x), "% missing": round(100 * s.isna().mean(), 1),
256	            "mean": x.mean(), "median": x.median(), "std": x.std(),
257	            "min": x.min(), "Q1": q1, "Q3": q3, "max": x.max(), "IQR": iqr, "skew": x.skew(),
258	            "# above Q3+1.5 IQR": int((x > q3 + 1.5 * iqr).sum()),
259	            "# below Q1-1.5 IQR": int((x < q1 - 1.5 * iqr).sum()),
260	        })
261	    out = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("field")
262	    out["skew flag"] = out["skew"].abs() > SKEW_FLAG
263	    return out

266	def category_profile(s, name, multi=False, names_hidden=False):
267	    # Levels, top level, and rare levels for a category; multi-label fields are split on commas
268	    n = s.notna().sum()
269	    vals = s.dropna().astype(str)
270	    if multi:
271	        vals = vals.str.split(",").explode().str.strip()
272	    vc = vals.value_counts()
273	    share = vc / n                                  # share of non-missing rows carrying each level
274	    row = {
275	        "field": name, "% missing": round(100 * s.isna().mean(), 1), "multi-label": multi,
276	        "levels": len(vc),
277	        "top level": "(person, withheld)" if names_hidden else vc.index[0],
278	        "top level % of rows": round(100 * share.iloc[0], 1),
279	        "levels < 5% of rows": int((share < RARE_FLAG).sum()),
280	        "% of rows in a level < 5%": None if multi else round(100 * share[share < RARE_FLAG].sum(), 1),
281	    }
282	    return row, vc
283

285	def id_text_profile(df, cols):
286	    # Identifiers and free text get uniqueness, duplicates and length, never averages
287	    rows = []
288	    for c in cols:
289	        s = df[c]
290	        nn = s.dropna().astype(str)
291	        rows.append({
292	            "field": c, "% missing": round(100 * s.isna().mean(), 1),
293	            "unique values": nn.nunique(),
294	            "rows sharing a value": int(nn.duplicated(keep=False).sum()),
295	            "median length (chars)": nn.str.len().median(),
296	        })
297	    return pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("field")

300	def box_hist(ax_box, ax_hist, x, title, xlabel, ylabel, log=False):
301	    # Box plot stacked over a histogram (Ch 6), with mean and median lines
302	    x = x.dropna().astype(float)
303	    if log and (x <= 0).any():
304	        title += f"\n({(x <= 0).sum():,} values <= 0 not shown on the log scale)"
305	        x = x[x > 0]
306	    bins = int(np.ceil(len(x) ** (1 / 3)))          # cube-root rule
307	    edges = np.logspace(np.log10(x.min()), np.log10(x.max()), bins + 1) if log else bins
308	    ax_hist.hist(x, bins=edges, color=BLUE, edgecolor="white", linewidth=0.4)
309	    ax_box.boxplot(x, orientation="horizontal", widths=0.6, patch_artist=True,
310	                   boxprops=dict(facecolor=BLUE_LIGHT, edgecolor=BLUE),
311	                   medianprops=dict(color=INK, linewidth=1.5),
312	                   whiskerprops=dict(color=BLUE), capprops=dict(color=BLUE),
313	                   flierprops=dict(marker="o", markersize=2.5, markerfacecolor=BLUE,
314	                                   markeredgecolor="none", alpha=0.35))
315	    ax_hist.axvline(x.median(), color=INK, lw=1, label=f"median {x.median():,.3g}")
316	    ax_hist.axvline(x.mean(), color=INK, lw=1, ls="--", label=f"mean {x.mean():,.3g}")
317	    if log:
318	        ax_hist.set_xscale("log")
319	    ax_box.set_yticks([])
320	    ax_box.grid(False)
321	    ax_box.set_title(title)
322	    ax_hist.set_xlabel(xlabel)
323	    ax_hist.set_ylabel(ylabel)
324	    ax_hist.legend(fontsize=7, frameon=False)

327	def profile_grid(specs, ylabel, ncols=3):
328	    # specs: list of (series, title, x-axis label, log scale?)
329	    nrows = int(np.ceil(len(specs) / ncols))
330	    fig = plt.figure(figsize=(4.3 * ncols, 3.1 * nrows), layout="constrained")
331	    subfigs = np.atleast_1d(fig.subfigures(nrows, ncols)).ravel()
332	    for sf, (x, title, xlabel, log) in zip(subfigs, specs):
333	        ax_box, ax_hist = sf.subplots(2, 1, sharex=True, height_ratios=[1, 4])
334	        box_hist(ax_box, ax_hist, x, title, xlabel, ylabel, log)
335	    plt.show()

338	def count_plot(ax, vc, n_rows, title, top=10, xlabel="% of rows"):
339	    # Horizontal bars sorted by frequency; dotted line = the 5% rare-level flag
340	    shares = (100 * vc / n_rows).head(top)[::-1]
341	    ax.barh(shares.index.astype(str), shares.values, color=BLUE, height=0.7)
342	    ax.axvline(100 * RARE_FLAG, color=INK2, ls=":", lw=1)
343	    for y, v in enumerate(shares.values):
344	        ax.text(v, y, f" {v:.1f}%", va="center", fontsize=7, color=INK2)
345	    ax.set_title(title + (f"  (top {top} of {len(vc):,})" if len(vc) > top else ""))
346	    ax.set_xlabel(xlabel)
347	    ax.grid(axis="y", visible=False)

814	##### [43] markdown
815	### 3j. What the profile shows (facts from the outputs above)
816	
817	**The label**
818	1. **Most films are money-losers at 2.5×:** 64.6% overall (train 65.2%, test 59.8%, stress 69.5%). The median film earns 1.59× its budget. Because losers are the majority, a 20% review capacity can hold at most about 31% of them. That's the ceiling on the contract's capture metric. The random baseline catches 20%.
819	2. **Some losses are data errors, not flops.** 24 films report revenue under $1,000, and 244 under $100,000. 179 films earned less than 1% of their budget. The lowest are obvious junk: "Aquajots" lists a $100M budget and $1 of revenue. At the other end, five films earned more than 100× their budget, and at least one looks like a typo: "Vacancy" (2018) shows $903M on a $1M budget. Left in, these errors inflate the loser rate.
820	3. **Possible double entries:** 6 pairs of TMDB ids share a title and year. Some look like the same film entered twice (e.g., "Diggy and The Bandits," with identical values). Others are different films with the same name (e.g., two "Blue Beetle" 2023 entries with different numbers).
821	
822	**Inputs allowed at the financing decision**
823	4. **Budget:** median $16M, mean $34M, skew 4.2. 4,330 of 5,766 budgets (75%) are round $1M figures, which suggests public estimates, not audited costs.
824	5. **Runtime:** 52 films have 0 (unknown), 36 are under 60 minutes, and the maximum is 999. Runtime is the final cut, not the planned one (weak link 4).
825	6. **Categories:** English is the original language of 73% of films, and the other 55 languages each fall under 5%. Drama appears on 46% of films; 5 of 19 genres are rare. **7,265 production companies, and 66% appear in only one film.** A company track record built from earlier films will be empty for most companies, and the same check is needed for directors after the join.
826	7. **Release month** is uneven: September has 12.1% of films and October 10.6%, against 8.3% if spread evenly.
827	
828	**Post-release and join fields**
829	8. **Vote fields:** 125 films have 0 votes and a 0 vote average. They're prohibited inputs and aren't used to filter the population. That's the earlier AI correction.
830	9. **RT movies:** `boxOffice` is 89.7% missing and every value that is present parses. 4,308 RT titles run under 40 minutes (shorts). 439 titles list streaming before theatrical release. RT has 64,718 directors; 65% have only one title, and 6.8% of titles list two or more directors.
831	10. **RT reviews:** `scoreSentiment` repeats `reviewState` on 100% of rows. `originalScore` mixes fractions, letter grades and blanks. 297 reviews point to an RT id that doesn't exist. 73,386 RT titles have no reviews at all.
832	
833	**Dispositions, the cleaning treatment for each flag, and the phase gate are decided by Matt** (Ch 6 decision gates) and recorded below once reviewed.
834	##### [44] markdown
835	### 3k. Dispositions and phase gate (approved by Matt Sorensen, 2026-11-18)
836	These are the next-phase treatments for each flag in 3i. **None are applied here.** Phase 3 (the cleaning ledger, step 13) carries them out and logs the row counts.
837	
838	| # | Flag | Evidence (3b–3h) | Disposition | Treatment in Phase 3 | Verification check |
839	|---|---|---|---|---|---|
840	| 1 | Revenue errors | 24 films report revenue < $1,000 and 244 < $100,000; 179 earned < 1% of budget | Requires repair | Hand-check a sample of films below 0.01×. Set a minimum revenue threshold, check it against RT box office for films that join, and run the analysis with and without these films. | Sample error rate; loser rate with vs. without the threshold |
841	| 2 | Extreme hits | 5 films above 100× (e.g., "Vacancy" 2018: $903M on $1M) | Requires source clarification | Hand-check all 5 and keep only the real ones. | Each one confirmed or excluded, with the reason |
842	| 3 | 64.6% losers at 2.5× | A 20% flag can catch at most about 31% of losers | Usable with a limitation | Keep the contract as is. State the 31% ceiling and lean on precision at 20%. Any change to the label needs a dated contract amendment. | Ceiling recomputed on the test films |
843	| 4 | Double ids | 6 pairs share a title and year | Requires repair | Same title, year, budget and revenue means the same film: keep one copy. Different values means different films: keep both. | Pair count before and after |
844	| 5 | Runtime | 52 zeros, 36 under 60 min, max 999 | Requires repair | Treat 0 and 999 as missing, with a missing-value indicator. Hand-check the under-60s. No invented values. | Count of missing runtimes after the rule |
845	| 6 | Round budgets | 75% are round $1M figures (likely estimates) | Usable with a limitation | No change. The budget-tier robustness check is already in the contract. | Model refit on budget tiers (Phase 4) |
846	| 7 | Rare categories | Language: English 73%, 55 others each < 5%. Country: US 68%. Genres: 5 of 19 rare. | Usable as defined, after grouping | Language: English vs. other. Country: US vs. other. All 19 genres kept, one yes/no column each. | Level counts after grouping |
847	| 8 | Thin track records | 66% of production companies appear in only one film | Usable with a limitation | Track record built from earlier films only, plus a "no earlier films" indicator. Director sparsity is checked after the join. | Share of films with no earlier films, by period |
848	| 9 | RT movies | 4,308 shorts; 439 titles with streaming before theatrical; `boxOffice` 89.7% missing | Usable with a limitation | Shorts drop out through the join. The date-order issue doesn't affect us. `boxOffice` is used only for the S4 check. | Join match counts (step 10) |
849	| 10 | RT reviews | `scoreSentiment` repeats `reviewState`; mixed `originalScore` formats; 297 orphan reviews | Not fit as model input | Drop `scoreSentiment` as redundant. Reviews are used only for the early-review test (step 11). | None needed |
850	| 11 | Vote fields | 125 films with 0 votes | Not fit for this decision | Not used: post-release, and filtering on them was the earlier AI correction. | None needed |
851	| 12 | Text and URL fields | Overview, tagline, homepage, poster and backdrop paths | Not fit for this decision | Not used; left out of the prepared file. | None needed |
852	
853	**Phase gate: CONTINUE** to step 10 (build and verify the RT join). The data supports the decision population, but the label needs the revenue repairs in rows 1–2 before modeling. The readiness verdict comes at step 12, after the S4 missing-revenue check.

## Claude  (2026-11-23T14:25:10.050Z)

Matt's Data Understanding now runs on the unified table, in `Edwards-A10.ipynb`. Committed and pushed.

**What matters most**
1. **The new films are mostly money-losers:** 79%, against 65% for Matt's TMDB-only films. That's good news. The extra sources are finding the flops TMDB was missing, which was the S4 worry. S4 is still triggered, though: 39% of films with a budget of at least $1M have no revenue from any source.
2. **The test set grew from 1,086 to 1,281 films,** which makes the 5-point bar easier to clear.
3. **The sources mostly agree:** budget and revenue 81–97%, runtime 92%, MPAA rating 99%. **Release dates don't:** they match in only 74% of films. TMDB often uses the first release anywhere (a festival or a foreign market), while the others use the US release. Release month is a model input, so we'll have to pick one.
4. **Every extra source covers big films much better than small ones.** For example, The Numbers covers 36% of films under $5M but 88% of films over $60M. Small films are where the losers are, so missing values aren't random.
5. **The new sources fix 220 of the films whose revenue was really domestic only.** Matt counted 396 of these films; it's 434 on the new table.

**Two bugs in the build notebook**
- It misses duplicates when one copy has runtime 0. For example, *Spider-Man: No Way Home* is still listed twice.
- The stefanoleone992 review file has about 121,000 duplicate rows, which inflates those review counts.

**Needs you and Matt:** section 3k has 10 draft decisions. The biggest is a **contract amendment** to allow financials from The Numbers and Wikidata. Another decides which extra inputs to allow (MPAA rating, source material, writer, cast).

Fix the two build bugs next?

## User  (2026-11-23T17:31:59.805Z)

Ya we should fix the bugs.  I wonder if adding a UID to the movie will help identify these duplicate issues better?

## Claude  (2026-11-23T17:32:14.414Z)

A UID would make films easier to *reference*, but it wouldn't *find* duplicates. The duplicates exist because one film got two different TMDB ids, so a new UID per row would just give each copy its own UID. What finds duplicates is an id that several sources share, and IMDb id is the only one we have.

A UID does fix a different problem, though. The negative ids for films only in The Numbers can change every time the table is rebuilt, so a hand-check that refers to them could later point at the wrong film. A stable `film_uid` would prevent that. More on that after the bug fixes.

## 7b. Critic reviews, rolled up to one row per film

Two review files, each keyed by an RT slug, so they attach through the RT links already on each film (no title matching):

| File | Attaches via | Prefix |
|---|---|---|
| `rotten_tomatoes_movie_reviews.csv` (1.44M) | `rt_id` (RT andrezaza join) | `rtrev_` |
| `stefanoleone992/rotten_tomatoes_critic_reviews.csv` (1.13M) | `sl_rotten_tomatoes_link` | `slrev_` |

Duplicate reviews are dropped first (repeated `reviewId` in the andrezaza file; exact duplicate rows in the stefanoleone992 file). Per film: review count, top-critic count, % fresh, first and last review date, and how many reviews are dated **before** the TMDB release date (plan step 11, "early buzz").

⚠️ Reviews are known only after release, except the before-release counts. **They're descriptive columns, not model inputs** (contract: no post-release inputs). Review text is not copied (license: short excerpts only).

--- cell 21 [code]
def rollup(rev, key, fresh, top, date, prefix, release):
    """One row per film key: counts, % fresh, date range, reviews dated before release."""
    r = pd.DataFrame({"key": rev[key], "fresh": fresh, "top": top.astype(bool),
                      "date": pd.to_datetime(rev[date], errors="coerce")})
    r = r.merge(release, on="key", how="inner")
    r["before"] = r["date"] < r["release_dt"]
    g = r.groupby("key").agg(n_reviews=("fresh", "size"), n_top_critic=("top", "sum"),
                             pct_fresh=("fresh", "mean"), first_review=("date", "min"),
                             last_review=("date", "max"), n_before_release=("before", "sum"))
    g["pct_fresh"] = (100 * g["pct_fresh"]).round(1)
    return g.add_prefix(prefix)


# RT andrezaza reviews -> rt_id

                    usecols=["id", "reviewId", "creationDate", "isTopCritic", "reviewState"])

rel_a = films.loc[films["rt_id"].notna(), ["rt_id", "release_dt"]].rename(columns={"rt_id": "key"})
agg_a = rollup(rev_a, "id", rev_a["reviewState"].eq("fresh"), rev_a["isTopCritic"], "creationDate", "rtrev_", rel_a)

--- cell 26 [markdown]
## 9. One row per film

The sources are joined one-to-one, but TMDB itself sometimes lists the same film twice (and junk entries repeat). Rows are merged when they are the same film by either rule:

1. **Same IMDb id** (`imdb_id`), or
2. **Same normalized title, release year within ±1, runtime within 5 minutes (or unknown on either side: TMDB uses 0 for unknown), and combined budget within 15%.** Title alone isn't enough: remakes and shorts share titles (*Trolls* 2016 at $125M vs a $30K short).

Within a group, the row with the most filled-in values is kept (TMDB rows and usable rows first), and its blanks are filled from the others. `merged_ids` lists the absorbed ids. `usable` is recomputed after merging.

--- cell 27 [code]
unified = films[films["year"].between(*YEARS) & (films["fin_budget"].notna() | films["fin_revenue"].notna())].copy()
unified = unified.reset_index(drop=True)

# Candidate pairs (row positions)
pairs = []
imdb = unified["imdb_id"].where(unified["imdb_id"].astype(str).str.startswith("tt"))
g = unified.assign(imdb=imdb).dropna(subset=["imdb"]).groupby("imdb").groups
pairs += [(ix[0], j) for ix in g.values() if len(ix) > 1 for j in ix[1:]]

k = pd.DataFrame({"pos": unified.index, "key": norm_title(unified["title"]), "year": unified["year"],
                  "rt": unified["runtime"].replace(0, np.nan), "b": unified["fin_budget"]})
k = k[k["key"].ne("")]
pp = k.merge(k, on="key", suffixes=("", "_2"))
runtime_ok = (pp["rt"] - pp["rt_2"]).abs().le(5) | pp["rt"].isna() | pp["rt_2"].isna()   # 0/missing = unknown
pp = pp[(pp["pos"] < pp["pos_2"]) & (pp["year"] - pp["year_2"]).abs().le(1) & runtime_ok
        & ((pp["b"] / pp["b_2"] - 1).abs() < 0.15)]
pairs += list(zip(pp["pos"], pp["pos_2"]))

# Group pairs (union-find)
parent = {}
def find(x):
    while parent.get(x, x) != x:
        x = parent[x]
    return x
for a, b in pairs:
    ra, rb = find(a), find(b)
    if ra != rb:
        parent[max(ra, rb)] = min(ra, rb)
groups = pd.Series({x: find(x) for x in set(np.ravel(pairs))}) if pairs else pd.Series(dtype=int)

unified["merged_ids"] = pd.NA
drop = []
filled = unified.notna().sum(axis=1)
for root, members in groups.groupby(groups).groups.items():
    rows = list(members)
    order = sorted(rows, key=lambda r: (unified.at[r, "in_tmdb"], unified.at[r, "usable"], filled[r]), reverse=True)
    keep, rest = order[0], order[1:]
    for r in rest:
        unified.loc[keep] = unified.loc[keep].combine_first(unified.loc[r])
    unified.at[keep, "merged_ids"] = ",".join(str(int(unified.at[r, "id"])) for r in rest)
    drop += rest

before_usable = unified["usable"].sum()
unified = unified.drop(index=drop).reset_index(drop=True)
unified["usable"] = (unified["year"].between(*YEARS) & unified["fin_budget"].ge(BUDGET_FLOOR)
                     & unified["fin_revenue"].gt(0))
assert unified["id"].is_unique
print(f"Merged {len(drop):,} duplicate rows into {groups.nunique() if len(groups) else 0:,} films "
      f"({len(pairs) - len(pp):,} pairs by IMDb id, {len(pp):,} by title/year/runtime/budget). "
      f"Usable: {before_usable:,} -> {unified['usable'].sum():,}")
display(unified.loc[unified["merged_ids"].notna() & unified["usable"], ["id", "title", "year", "fin_budget", "merged_ids"]])

unified.to_csv(CLEAN / "films_unified.csv", index=False)

      f"({unified['usable'].sum():,} usable, {(~unified['in_tmdb']).sum():,} not in TMDB)")
