````
--- cell 0 [markdown]
# 00 · Build the unified dataset

**Shared pipeline notebook (team-owned).** Run it once after `tools/get_data.py`, and again whenever this notebook or the raw data changes. Changes go through a PR.

**Output:** `data/clean/films_unified.csv`, **one row per film** with every source attached. All other notebooks start from this file instead of re-merging. It is gitignored, so each person builds their own copy.

| Source | Adds | Join |
|---|---|---|
| TMDB | Base table: one row per TMDB id | — |
| The Numbers | Budget, **worldwide** gross, MPAA, source, franchise, companies | Title + year matcher (§4), hand-checked 50/50 |
| Wikidata snapshot (committed) | Budget and box office in USD | TMDB id |
| Box Office Mojo | Domestic gross, theaters (US theatrical run) | Title + year matcher |
| RT stefanoleone992 | `actors`, `production_company` | Title + year matcher |
| RT andrezaza | Director, writer, RT box office, ratings | Matt's join rules (§7), hand-checked 0/50 wrong |

**Combined financials:** `fin_budget` / `fin_revenue` take the first available value from TMDB → The Numbers → Wikidata; `fin_*_src` records which. `usable` = 2000–2023, budget ≥ $1M, revenue > 0.

Rows not in TMDB (The Numbers only) have a **negative `id`** and `in_tmdb` = False.

Column prefixes: none = TMDB, `tn_` The Numbers, `wd_` Wikidata, `bom_` Box Office Mojo, `sl_` RT stefanoleone992, `rt_` RT andrezaza, `fin_` combined.

--- cell 1 [markdown]
## 1. Setup

--- cell 2 [code]
import unicodedata
from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

pd.set_option("display.max_columns", 60)
pd.set_option("display.width", 200)

RAW = Path("../data/raw")
CLEAN = Path("../data/clean")
YEARS = (2000, 2023)          # contract window
BUDGET_FLOOR = 1_000_000      # contract floor

--- cell 3 [markdown]
## 2. TMDB

All released, non-adult films (one row per id). Matching uses a wider year window (1998–2025) so films near the edges can still match; the contract window is applied after.

--- cell 4 [code]
t = pd.read_csv(RAW / "TMDB_movie_dataset_v11.csv", low_memory=False)
t["release_dt"] = pd.to_datetime(t["release_date"], errors="coerce")
t["year"] = t["release_dt"].dt.year
tmdb = t[t["status"].eq("Released") & ~t["adult"] & t["year"].between(1998, 2025)].drop_duplicates("id").copy()

# Sanity check: Matt's contract population is reproduced exactly
pop = tmdb[tmdb["year"].between(*YEARS) & tmdb["budget"].ge(BUDGET_FLOOR) & tmdb["revenue"].gt(0)]
assert len(pop) == 5766, len(pop)
print(f"TMDB candidates for matching: {len(tmdb):,}; contract population: {len(pop):,}")

--- cell 5 [markdown]
## 3. Load the other sources

--- cell 6 [code]
tn = pd.read_csv(RAW / "the_numbers/Top Movies (Cleaned Data).csv", low_memory=False)
tn["year"] = pd.to_datetime(tn["Release Date"], errors="coerce").dt.year
tn = tn[tn["year"].between(*YEARS)].reset_index(drop=True)

wd = pd.read_csv(RAW / "wikidata/wikidata_film_financials_2026-11-21.csv")
wd = wd.rename(columns={"tmdb": "id"}).drop_duplicates("id")

bom_daily = pd.read_csv(RAW / "boxofficemojo/revenues_per_day.csv.gz", parse_dates=["date"])
# `id` in this file is per ROW (film-day), not per film: collapse to one row per title
bom = (bom_daily.groupby("title")
       .agg(first_date=("date", "min"), domestic_gross=("revenue", "sum"),
            days=("date", "nunique"), max_theaters=("theaters", "max"), distributor=("distributor", "first"))
       .reset_index())
bom["year"] = bom["first_date"].dt.year

sl = pd.read_csv(RAW / "stefanoleone992/rotten_tomatoes_movies.csv", low_memory=False)
sl["year"] = pd.to_datetime(sl["original_release_date"], errors="coerce").dt.year

pd.Series({"The Numbers (2000-23)": len(tn), "Wikidata": len(wd), "Box Office Mojo titles": len(bom),
           "RT stefanoleone992": len(sl)}, name="rows").to_frame()

--- cell 7 [markdown]
## 4. Title + year matcher

1. **Normalize titles:** strip accents, lowercase, `&` → `and`, drop a leading *The / A / An*, keep letters and digits only.
2. **Candidates:** same normalized title as TMDB's `title` **or** `original_title`, release year within ±2.
3. **Pick the best candidate** per source film: budget agrees (±15%), then closest year, then closest runtime, then most TMDB votes (votes only break ties for identity; they're never a model input).
4. **Year differences need corroboration:** if years differ, runtime must be within 10 minutes or the budget must agree.
5. **One-to-one only:** a TMDB film claimed by two source films is dropped from both.

--- cell 8 [code]
def norm_title(s: pd.Series) -> pd.Series:
    s = s.fillna("").astype(str).map(lambda x: unicodedata.normalize("NFKD", x).encode("ascii", "ignore").decode())
    s = s.str.lower().str.replace("&", " and ", regex=False)
    s = s.str.replace(r"^(the|a|an)\s+", "", regex=True)
    return s.str.replace(r"[^a-z0-9]", "", regex=True)


tmdb_keys = pd.concat([
    tmdb.assign(key=norm_title(tmdb["title"])),
    tmdb.assign(key=norm_title(tmdb["original_title"])),
]).drop_duplicates(["id", "key"])
tmdb_keys = tmdb_keys.loc[tmdb_keys["key"].ne(""), ["id", "key", "year", "runtime", "budget", "vote_count"]]


def match_to_tmdb(src, title_col, runtime_col=None, budget_col=None, name="src", keys=None):
    """Return src_row -> film id, one-to-one, with match diagnostics. `keys` defaults to all TMDB films."""
    keys = tmdb_keys if keys is None else keys
    s = pd.DataFrame({"src_row": np.arange(len(src)), "key": norm_title(src[title_col]), "src_year": src["year"]})
    s["src_runtime"] = src[runtime_col] if runtime_col else np.nan
    s["src_budget"] = src[budget_col] if budget_col else np.nan
    m = s.merge(keys, on="key")
    m["year_diff"] = (m["src_year"] - m["year"]).abs()
    m = m[m["year_diff"] <= 2]
    m["runtime_diff"] = (m["src_runtime"] - m["runtime"]).abs()
    m["budget_agrees"] = m["budget"].gt(0) & ((m["budget"] / m["src_budget"] - 1).abs() < 0.15)
    m = (m.sort_values(["src_row", "budget_agrees", "year_diff", "runtime_diff", "vote_count"],
                       ascending=[True, False, True, True, False], na_position="last")
          .drop_duplicates("src_row"))
    m = m[m["year_diff"].eq(0) | m["runtime_diff"].le(10) | m["budget_agrees"]]
    m = m[~m["id"].duplicated(keep=False)]
    print(f"{name:<12} matched {len(m):,} of {len(src):,} ({len(m) / len(src):.0%}); "
          f"year diff counts {m['year_diff'].value_counts().sort_index().to_dict()}")
    return m[["src_row", "id", "year_diff", "runtime_diff", "budget_agrees"]]


tn_match = match_to_tmdb(tn, "Movie Name", "Running Time (minutes)", "Production Budget (USD)", "The Numbers")
bom_match = match_to_tmdb(bom, "title", name="Box Office Mojo")
sl_match = match_to_tmdb(sl, "movie_title", "runtime", name="RT sl")

both = tn_match.merge(tmdb[["id", "budget"]], on="id")
both = both[both["budget"].gt(0)]
print(f"\nCheck: where TMDB and The Numbers both have a budget, they agree (±15%) for "
      f"{both['budget_agrees'].mean():.0%} of {len(both):,} matched films")

--- cell 9 [markdown]
## 5. Attach the sources to TMDB

--- cell 10 [code]
def attach(base, src, match, prefix, cols):
    part = src.iloc[match["src_row"]][cols].set_axis(match["id"].values)
    part.columns = [f"{prefix}_{c}" for c in cols]
    part[f"{prefix}_year_diff"] = match["year_diff"].values
    return base.merge(part, left_on="id", right_index=True, how="left")


# Every column from each source (except its own id / derived year)
tn_cols = [c for c in tn.columns if c not in ("id", "year")]
bom_cols = [c for c in bom.columns if c != "year"]
sl_cols = [c for c in sl.columns if c != "year"]
films = tmdb.copy()
films = attach(films, tn, tn_match, "tn", tn_cols)
films = attach(films, bom, bom_match, "bom", bom_cols)
films = attach(films, sl, sl_match, "sl", sl_cols)
films = films.merge(wd.add_prefix("wd_").rename(columns={"wd_id": "id"}), on="id", how="left")
assert films["id"].is_unique
print(f"{films.shape[1]} columns after attaching The Numbers ({len(tn_cols)}), Box Office Mojo ({len(bom_cols)}), "
      f"RT stefanoleone992 ({len(sl_cols)}), Wikidata ({wd.shape[1] - 1})")

--- cell 11 [markdown]
## 6. Combined budget and revenue

First non-missing value wins: TMDB → The Numbers → Wikidata. Zero means missing in every source.

--- cell 12 [code]
def first_valid(*cols):
    vals = pd.concat([c.where(c > 0) for c, _ in cols], axis=1)
    src = pd.Series(pd.NA, index=vals.index, dtype="string")
    for i, (_, label) in reversed(list(enumerate(cols))):
        src = src.mask(vals.iloc[:, i].notna(), label)
    return vals.bfill(axis=1).iloc[:, 0], src


films["fin_budget"], films["fin_budget_src"] = first_valid(
    (films["budget"], "tmdb"), (films["tn_Production Budget (USD)"], "the_numbers"), (films["wd_wd_budget_usd"], "wikidata"))
films["fin_revenue"], films["fin_revenue_src"] = first_valid(
    (films["revenue"], "tmdb"), (films["tn_Worldwide Gross (USD)"], "the_numbers"), (films["wd_wd_box_office_usd"], "wikidata"))

films["usable"] = (films["year"].between(*YEARS) & films["fin_budget"].ge(BUDGET_FLOOR) & films["fin_revenue"].gt(0))
usable = films[films["usable"]]
print(f"Usable films: {len(usable):,} (TMDB alone: {len(pop):,}, +{len(usable) - len(pop):,})")
pd.crosstab(usable["fin_budget_src"], usable["fin_revenue_src"], margins=True)

--- cell 13 [markdown]
## 6c. Add The Numbers films that have no TMDB match

406 The Numbers films (2000–2023) didn't match any TMDB film. They're added as their own rows so the table covers every film we have financials for. They have The Numbers fields (budget, gross, MPAA, genre, companies…) but no TMDB fields.

- **Duplicate guard:** a film is *not* added if TMDB already has a film with the same normalized title within ±1 year (and any financial value). The matcher in §4 rejected those pairs only because nothing corroborated the year difference (e.g. *Jason X*: 2002 vs 2001, budgets $14M vs $11M); they're the same film, and keeping both would count it twice. A second guard in §7 drops any that share an RT record with a TMDB film (catches bigger year gaps, e.g. a 2001 Hong Kong release vs a 2004 US release).
- **`id` is negative** for these rows (−1, −2, …): there's no TMDB id. `in_tmdb` = False marks them.
- `title`, `year`, `release_dt` and `runtime` are filled from The Numbers so the RT join (§7) can match them too.
- `fin_*` come from The Numbers; `usable` uses the same rule as every other film.

--- cell 14 [code]
tn_new = tn.drop(index=tn_match["src_row"])

# Duplicate guard: same normalized title as a TMDB film with financials, year within +/-1
has_fin = films["year"].between(*YEARS) & (films["fin_budget"].notna() | films["fin_revenue"].notna())
tk = films.loc[has_fin, ["title", "original_title", "year"]]
tmdb_titles = pd.concat([pd.DataFrame({"key": norm_title(tk[c]), "y": tk["year"]}) for c in ["title", "original_title"]])
probe = pd.DataFrame({"key": norm_title(tn_new["Movie Name"]), "y": tn_new["year"]}, index=tn_new.index)
hits = probe.reset_index().merge(tmdb_titles, on="key", suffixes=("", "_t"))
dup_idx = hits.loc[(hits["y"] - hits["y_t"]).abs() <= 1, "index"].unique()
print(f"Not added (probable duplicates of TMDB films): {len(dup_idx)}")
tn_new = tn_new.drop(index=dup_idx).reset_index(drop=True)
rows = tn_new[tn_cols].add_prefix("tn_")
rows.insert(0, "id", -(np.arange(len(tn_new)) + 1))
rows["title"] = tn_new["Movie Name"].values
rows["original_title"] = tn_new["Movie Name"].values
rows["release_dt"] = pd.to_datetime(tn_new["Release Date"], errors="coerce").values
rows["year"] = tn_new["year"].values
rows["runtime"] = tn_new["Running Time (minutes)"].values
rows["tn_year_diff"] = 0
rows["fin_budget"] = rows["tn_Production Budget (USD)"].where(rows["tn_Production Budget (USD)"] > 0)
rows["fin_revenue"] = rows["tn_Worldwide Gross (USD)"].where(rows["tn_Worldwide Gross (USD)"] > 0)
rows["fin_budget_src"] = rows["fin_budget"].notna().map({True: "the_numbers", False: pd.NA})
rows["fin_revenue_src"] = rows["fin_revenue"].notna().map({True: "the_numbers", False: pd.NA})
rows["usable"] = rows["year"].between(*YEARS) & rows["fin_budget"].ge(BUDGET_FLOOR) & rows["fin_revenue"].gt(0)
rows["in_tmdb"] = False

films["in_tmdb"] = True
before = films["usable"].sum()
films = pd.concat([films, rows], ignore_index=True)
assert films["id"].is_unique
print(f"Added {len(rows):,} The Numbers-only films ({rows['usable'].sum():,} usable). "
      f"Usable films: {before:,} -> {films['usable'].sum():,}")

--- cell 15 [markdown]
## 6d. Match Box Office Mojo and RT stefanoleone992 to The Numbers-only films

§4 matched these two sources to TMDB films only. The Numbers-only films are matched here with the same matcher, against source records that weren't already used (keeps every source record on at most one film).

--- cell 16 [code]
new = films[~films["in_tmdb"]]
new_keys = pd.DataFrame({"id": new["id"], "key": norm_title(new["title"]), "year": new["year"],
                         "runtime": new["runtime"], "budget": new["fin_budget"], "vote_count": 0})


def fill_from(src, used_rows, title_col, runtime_col, prefix, cols, name):
    global films
    pool = src.drop(index=used_rows).reset_index(drop=True)
    m = match_to_tmdb(pool, title_col, runtime_col, name=name, keys=new_keys)
    part = pool.iloc[m["src_row"]][cols].set_axis(m["id"].values)
    part.columns = [f"{prefix}_{c}" for c in cols]
    part[f"{prefix}_year_diff"] = m["year_diff"].values
    idx = films.index[films["id"].isin(part.index)]
    films.loc[idx, part.columns] = part.loc[films.loc[idx, "id"]].values


fill_from(bom, bom_match["src_row"], "title", None, "bom", bom_cols, "BOM -> TN-only")
fill_from(sl, sl_match["src_row"], "movie_title", "runtime", "sl", sl_cols, "RT sl -> TN-only")

--- cell 17 [markdown]
## 7. RT movies (andrezaza): director, writer, RT box office

Uses **Matt's join rules exactly** (`Sorensen-A10.ipynb` §4, hand-checked 0/50 wrong): normalized title (`title`, then `original_title`), RT year within ±1, or rule 2b (streaming-only RT date later than release, runtime within 5 min); best candidate = title before original_title, rule 2 before 2b, closest year, closest runtime; one-to-one, ambiguous pairs dropped.

Matt ran it on the 5,766-film population. Here it runs on every 2000–2023 film with any financial value, after first checking that the same code reproduces his 4,673 pairs.

--- cell 18 [code]
def matt_norm(s):
    s = s.fillna("").astype(str).map(lambda x: unicodedata.normalize("NFKD", x).encode("ascii", "ignore").decode())
    s = s.str.lower().str.replace("&", " and ", regex=False)
    s = s.str.replace(r"[^a-z0-9 ]", " ", regex=True)
    return s.str.replace(r"\s+", " ", regex=True).str.strip()


def parse_money(s):
    m = s.str.extract(r"^\$([\d.]+)([KMB]?)$")
    return m[0].astype(float) * m[1].map({"": 1, "K": 1e3, "M": 1e6, "B": 1e9})


rt_movies = pd.read_csv(RAW / "rotten_tomatoes_movies.csv", low_memory=False)
rtj = rt_movies.drop_duplicates("id").copy()
rt_theat = pd.to_datetime(rtj["releaseDateTheaters"], errors="coerce").dt.year
rt_stream = pd.to_datetime(rtj["releaseDateStreaming"], errors="coerce").dt.year
rtj["rt_year"] = rt_theat.fillna(rt_stream)
rtj["rt_year_source"] = np.where(rt_theat.notna(), "theatrical", np.where(rt_stream.notna(), "streaming", "none"))
rtj["key"] = matt_norm(rtj["title"])
rtj = rtj[rtj["key"].ne("") & rtj["rt_year"].notna()]


def rt_join(tj):
    """Matt's §4 rules. tj needs id, title, original_title, year, runtime. Returns the 1:1 crosswalk."""
    tj = tj.assign(key_title=matt_norm(tj["title"]), key_orig=matt_norm(tj["original_title"]))
    side = rtj[["id", "key", "rt_year", "rt_year_source", "runtimeMinutes"]].rename(columns={"id": "rt_id"})
    cands = []
    for key_col, how in [("key_title", "title"), ("key_orig", "original_title")]:
        c = tj[["id", "year", "runtime", key_col]].merge(side, left_on=key_col, right_on="key")
        cands.append(c.assign(matched_on=how))
    cands = pd.concat(cands, ignore_index=True)
    signed = cands["rt_year"] - cands["year"]
    cands["year_diff"] = signed.abs()
    cands["runtime_diff"] = (cands["runtimeMinutes"] - cands["runtime"].replace(0, np.nan)).abs()
    rule2 = cands["year_diff"] <= 1
    rule2b = (cands["rt_year_source"] == "streaming") & (signed > 1) & (cands["runtime_diff"] <= 5)
    cands["rule"] = np.where(rule2, "2: year +/-1", np.where(rule2b, "2b: later streaming + runtime", None))
    cands = cands[rule2 | rule2b].copy()
    cands["title_rank"] = cands["matched_on"].map({"title": 0, "original_title": 1})
    cands["rule_rank"] = cands["rule"].str.startswith("2b").astype(int)
    cands = cands.sort_values(["id", "title_rank", "rule_rank", "year_diff", "runtime_diff"], na_position="last")
    best = cands.drop_duplicates("id")
    return best[~best["rt_id"].duplicated(keep=False)][["id", "rt_id", "matched_on", "rule", "year_diff", "runtime_diff"]]


# 1) Same code on Matt's population must give his 4,673 pairs
assert len(rt_join(pop)) == 4673, "doesn't reproduce Matt's crosswalk"

# 2) Three passes, so verified films get first claim on each RT record:
#    usable TMDB films -> usable The Numbers-only films -> all other 2000-2023 films
scope = films["year"].between(*YEARS) & (films["fin_budget"].notna() | films["fin_revenue"].notna())
passes = [films["usable"] & films["in_tmdb"], films["usable"] & ~films["in_tmdb"], scope & ~films["usable"]]
taken, parts = set(), []
for mask in passes:
    xw = rt_join(films[mask])
    xw = xw[~xw["rt_id"].isin(taken)]
    taken |= set(xw["rt_id"])
    parts.append(xw)
rt_xw = pd.concat(parts, ignore_index=True)
assert rt_xw["id"].is_unique and rt_xw["rt_id"].is_unique

# The Numbers-only films whose RT match was already claimed by a TMDB film: probably the same film
tn_side = rt_join(films[passes[1]])
dup_suspects = tn_side[tn_side["rt_id"].isin(parts[0]["rt_id"])]

matt_pairs = rt_join(pop)
kept = parts[0].merge(matt_pairs, on=["id", "rt_id"]).shape[0]
print(f"RT matches: {len(parts[0]):,} usable TMDB + {len(parts[1]):,} usable The Numbers-only + {len(parts[2]):,} other. "
      f"Matt's verified pairs kept: {kept:,} of {len(matt_pairs):,}")
# Second duplicate guard: sharing an RT record with a TMDB film means it's the same film
# (e.g. Shaolin Soccer: 2001 Hong Kong release vs 2004 US release in The Numbers)
films = films[~films["id"].isin(dup_suspects["id"])]
print(f"Dropped {len(dup_suspects)} The Numbers-only films that share an RT record with a TMDB film (duplicates)")

--- cell 19 [code]
rt_cols = [c for c in rt_movies.columns if c != "id"]
rt_part = (rt_xw.merge(rtj[["id"] + rt_cols].rename(columns={"id": "rt_id"}), on="rt_id")
               .assign(boxOffice_usd=lambda d: parse_money(d["boxOffice"])))
rt_part = rt_part.set_index("id").add_prefix("rt_").rename(columns={"rt_rt_id": "rt_id"})
films = films.drop(columns=[c for c in films.columns if c.startswith("rt_")]).merge(
    rt_part, left_on="id", right_index=True, how="left")
assert films["id"].is_unique
films.loc[films["usable"], ["rt_id", "rt_director", "rt_writer", "rt_boxOffice_usd"]].notna().mean().map("{:.0%}".format)
````

````
# A10: Data Understanding on the unified dataset (Tanner Edwards)

Personal notebook. Re-runs Matt's Data Understanding (`Sorensen-A10.ipynb` §2–§3, plan steps 8–9) on the **unified dataset** built by `00_build_dataset.ipynb`, which adds four sources and grows the usable population from 5,766 to about 6,900 films. Same helpers, same review flags, same privacy rule.

**Run `00_build_dataset.ipynb` first.** This notebook only reads `data/clean/films_unified.csv` and the raw files; it writes nothing.

| Section | What | Matt's equivalent |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Setup and Matt's profile helpers | §1, §3 helpers |
| 2 | Data Receipt for the **new** sources | §2 |
| 3a | Field inventory: all columns, role at the financing decision | §3a |
| 3b | The label on the expanded population | §3b |
| 3c–3f | Numeric, categorical, identifier/text and date fields | §3c–§3h |
| 3g | **New:** do the sources agree with each other? | — |
| 3h | **New:** who has which data (coverage by period and budget tier) | §4a idea |
| 3i | Flag register | §3i |
| 3j–3k | Findings and proposed dispositions (need Tanner + Matt sign-off) | §3j–§3k |

This section **observes and records; it doesn't clean.**

=== md cell 5
## 2. Data Receipt for the new sources (plan step 8)

Matt's §2 covers TMDB, RT movies (andrezaza) and RT reviews. These are the sources added since. Licenses were read from the Kaggle API (`licenseName`) and the GitHub API on 2026-11-23.

| Field | The Numbers | Box Office Mojo | Wikidata snapshot | RT movies (stefanoleone992) | RT critic reviews (stefanoleone992) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **File** | `the_numbers/Top Movies (Cleaned Data).csv` | `boxofficemojo/revenues_per_day.csv.gz` | `wikidata/wikidata_film_financials_2026-11-21.csv` | `stefanoleone992/rotten_tomatoes_movies.csv` | `stefanoleone992/rotten_tomatoes_critic_reviews.csv` |
| **Publisher** | michaelmatta0 (Kaggle) | tjwaterman99 (GitHub release) | Our own SPARQL query (`tools/wikidata_films.rq`) | stefanoleone992 (Kaggle) | same |
| **Original source** | the-numbers.com (Nash Information Services) | boxofficemojo.com (IMDb) | Wikidata (Wikimedia, crowd-edited) | Rotten Tomatoes | Rotten Tomatoes |
| **URL** | kaggle.com/datasets/michaelmatta0/movies-ultimate-metrics-features-and-metadata | github.com/tjwaterman99/boxofficemojo-scraper | query.wikidata.org | kaggle.com/datasets/stefanoleone992/rotten-tomatoes-movies-and-critic-reviews-dataset | same |
| **Access date** | 2026-11-21 | 2026-11-20 | 2026-11-21 (snapshot committed to git) | 2026-11-20 | 2026-11-20 |
| **License (as stated)** | MIT | **None stated** | CC0 1.0 | CC0 1.0 | CC0 1.0 |
| **Claimed grain** | One row per film | One row per film **per day** | One row per film with a USD budget and a TMDB id | One row per RT film (link) | One row per critic review |
| **Population** | ~6.6k "top" films by budget, all years | Films on the US daily chart, 2000–2025 | Wikidata films 2000–2023 with a USD cost | ~17.7k RT films (2020 scrape) | Reviews of those films |
| **Sensitive fields** | None | None | None | `directors`, `authors`, `actors`: public professionals | `critic_name`, `review_content`: named people and copyrighted text |
| **Rights caveats** | Scraped; The Numbers' terms aren't overridden by the uploader's MIT | Scraped; no license, so academic fair use only | — | Scores belong to RT | Review text is copyrighted; not copied into the unified file |
| **Permitted use here** | Academic, non-commercial. Cite the-numbers.com. | Same, and cite Box Office Mojo | Cite Wikidata | Same as Matt's RT files | Same; counts only |

**Also note:** `get_data.py` downloads `rotten_tomatoes_movie_reviews.csv` from **priyamchoksi** (license MIT), while Matt's receipt cites the **andrezaza** upload (CC0). Same row count (1,444,963). The receipt should cite one; open question for Matt.

=== md cell 14
## 3. Univariate profile of every field (plan step 9)

**Which rows:** the usable films (2000–2023, budget ≥ $1M, revenue > 0 from any source), the population the screen will score. The label is shown by period. **Review flags (Ch 6):** |skew| > 0.5; any category level held by < 5% of non-missing rows. **Privacy:** director, writer, actor and critic names are profiled by counts only.

=== md cell 18
### 3b. The label on the expanded population
Money-loser = combined revenue < 2.5 × combined budget, with 1×, 2×, 3× sensitivity. Compared with Matt's TMDB-only figures (64.6% losers overall), and split by where the financials came from.

=== md cell 22
### 3d. Categorical fields
Multi-label fields are split on commas, so shares add to more than 100%. Person fields (director, writer, actors) show counts only.

=== md cell 28
### 3g. Do the sources agree? (new)

Where two sources report the same thing, they should agree. Disagreement is either a wrong match or a data error, and it tells Phase 3 which source to trust. Agreement = within 15% for money, 5 minutes for runtime, 7 days for release dates, same label for MPAA.

=== md cell 30
### 3h. Who has which data? (new)
Matt found the RT join covers big films better than small ones (58% of $1–5M vs 91% of $60M+). The same check for every source and key input, by period and budget tier. Uneven coverage means missing values aren't random, so Phase 3 needs "unknown" indicators, not dropped rows.

=== md cell 34
### 3j. What the profile shows (facts from the outputs above, run 2026-11-23)

**Population and the label**
1. **6,928 usable films** (train 5,020 · test 1,281 · stress 627), up from Matt's 5,766. The test set grows 18% (1,086 → 1,281), which tightens the bootstrap CI on the evidence standard.
2. **The added films are mostly losers.** Films whose budget or revenue came from The Numbers or Wikidata are 79% losers at 2.5×, against 65% for Matt's TMDB-only films. Overall: 67.1% (Matt 64.6%). This is the S4 worry in reverse: the extra sources recover some of the flops TMDB was missing. The 20%-capacity ceiling drops slightly, from 31% to 30% of losers.
3. **S4 is still triggered.** 38.7% of films with a budget ≥ $1M still have no revenue from any source (Matt: 43.6%), and 52% in the stress years.
4. **Junk values grew with the population.** 268 films earn < 1% of budget (Matt 179), 35 report revenue < $1,000, 379 < $100,000. The lowest are the same junk Matt found (*Aquajots*: $100M budget, $1 revenue). Six films above 100×, including *Vacancy* (2018, $903M on $1M) and a new one, *Space Station 3D*, where a Wikidata budget meets a TMDB revenue.

**Do the sources agree?** (new)
5. **Money mostly agrees.** Budget: TMDB vs The Numbers 85%, TMDB vs Wikidata 90% (within 15%). Worldwide revenue: 81–87%. Domestic gross across The Numbers, Box Office Mojo and RT: 92–97%. Runtime: 92–93% within 5 minutes. MPAA rating: the three sources agree on 99%.
6. **Release dates often don't.** TMDB's date is within 7 days of The Numbers / Box Office Mojo for only 74–75% of films. TMDB often records the first release anywhere (a festival or a foreign market); the others record the US release. Release month is an allowed input, so Phase 3 has to pick one definition.
7. **Matt's domestic-as-worldwide risk is larger than first counted:** 434 films (Matt: 396) have TMDB revenue equal to RT domestic. **The Numbers has a higher worldwide figure for 220 of them**, a direct repair.

**Coverage is uneven** (new)
8. **Every extra source covers big films far better than small ones.** The Numbers matches 36% of $1–5M films vs 88% of $60M+; MPAA and source material 34–35% vs 88%; director 61% vs 88%; franchise 3% vs 42%. Small films are where most losers are, so a missing value is not random. RT stefanoleone992 (scraped in 2020) has actors for only 5% of stress-period films.
9. **Franchise is thin and partly garbled:** 14% coverage; 92 of 1,004 values look like several franchise names run together (e.g. "BatmanDark Knight Trilogy").
10. **Track records are sparse:** 63% of directors and 67% of production companies appear in only one usable film.

**Keys and duplicates**
11. **Duplicates (fixed in the build, 2026-11-23).** The first profile found title+year pairs that were the same film entered twice (*Spider-Man: No Way Home*, *Timber Falls*): the build's rule required runtime within 5 minutes, and one copy had runtime 0. The rule now treats 0 as unknown, which also caught *WALL·E* and *Black Panther: Wakanda Forever*. 3 pairs remain and are **not** duplicates: *Underdogs* (two different 2013 films), *Uncharted 2* (a video game, entered twice) and a junk *Blue Beetle* entry ($400M revenue, runtime 0). Those are cleaning issues. 2 usable films share a Wikidata item.
12. **Review duplicates (fixed in the build).** The stefanoleone992 review file had 120,945 exact duplicate rows and the andrezaza file 12,394 repeated review ids; both are dropped before the rollups.

**Raw-file notes:** The Numbers has 150 release dates after the access date (up to 2068); none reach the usable population. RT sl reviews have 83 placeholder dates (1800-01-01). The Box Office Mojo scraper has no license.

=== md cell 35
### 3k. Proposed dispositions and phase gate (DRAFT, pending Tanner + Matt sign-off)

Matt's §3k rows 1–12 still apply. These are the additions for the unified dataset. **None are applied here.**

| # | Flag | Evidence | Proposed disposition | Treatment | Verification |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| U1 | Population now multi-source | 6,931 films; 1,168 use The Numbers / Wikidata financials | Requires a contract amendment | Dated amendment: population = 2000–2023, budget ≥ $1M, revenue > 0 **from TMDB, The Numbers or Wikidata**, with source precedence stated | Amendment recorded in the contract file |
| U2 | Added films skew to losers | 79% vs 65% losers | Usable; report it | Report results on the full population and on Matt's TMDB-only population as a sensitivity check | Capture on both populations |
| U3 | Domestic-as-worldwide revenue | 434 films; The Numbers higher for 220 | Requires repair | Replace TMDB revenue with The Numbers worldwide where TMDB = RT domestic and The Numbers is higher. Flag the other 214. | Loser rate before / after |
| U4 | Source disagreement on budget / revenue | 81–90% agree within 15% | Requires a rule | Keep precedence TMDB → The Numbers → Wikidata, but hand-check films where they disagree by > 2× | Hand-check sample error rate |
| U5 | Release date definitions differ | 74% agree within 7 days | Requires a rule | Use the US release date (The Numbers / Box Office Mojo) where available, TMDB otherwise; keep the source | Month distribution before / after |
| U6 | Coverage skews by budget | The Numbers 36% vs 88%; director 61% vs 88% | Usable with a limitation | Every optional input gets an "unknown" indicator; no dropped rows | Loser rate by known / unknown |
| U7 | Leftover duplicates | Runtime 0 blocked the merge rule | **Done** (build, 2026-11-23) | Runtime 0 counts as unknown; 4 more films merged | 3 same-title pairs left, none duplicates |
| U8 | Review duplicates | 120,945 + 12,394 duplicate reviews | **Done** (build, 2026-11-23) | Dropped before the rollups | Counts reported in the build |
| U11 | Junk entries | *Uncharted 2* (video game), *Blue Beetle* copy with $400M revenue and runtime 0 | Requires repair | Cleaning rule for runtime-0 TMDB entries that collide with a real film | Pair count after cleaning |
| U9 | Franchise field | 14% coverage, 92 garbled values | Investigate | See `FEATURE_IDEAS.md` (sequel / franchise); likely needs Wikidata series data | Coverage after |
| U10 | Candidate inputs not in the contract | MPAA, source, creative type, writer, cast, franchise | Needs a decision | Decide which to add by amendment before Phase 3 features | Decision recorded |

**Proposed phase gate: CONTINUE**, after U1 (amendment). Build fixes U7 and U8 are done. The S4 readiness verdict still belongs to step 12.
````

## Claude  (2026-11-24T04:09:59.599Z)

Yes, look at missing values first. Two reasons:

1. **"Missing" looks different in each source.** TMDB uses `0` for unknown budget, revenue and runtime. Some text fields are empty strings, and RT reviews have placeholder dates like `1800-01-01`. If you combine columns before cleaning those up, a fake `0` can override a real value from another source.
2. **The gaps decide how to combine.** If The Numbers fills most of the films where TMDB is blank, you combine those two columns. If they both miss the same films, a combined column adds nothing.

**Proposed approach:**
- Define "missing" for each column: NaN, empty, `0` where 0 is impossible, and placeholders.
- Group the repeat columns by concept: runtime, rating, genre, release date, director, companies, critic score, budget, revenue.
- For each concept, build one table showing how often each source is filled, and how full a combined column would be.

That table tells you which columns to merge, which to drop, and which concepts stay thin even after combining.

One question before I build it: **should this cover only the 6,838 usable films (the ones the model will use), or all 45,492 rows?** I'd recommend usable films only.

one clarifying qeustion, did we do cleaning to only include films that made more than $1m or had that high of a budget?

## Claude  (2026-11-24T04:14:33.545Z)

The **budget** has to be at least $1M. Box office only has to be **above $0**, so a film can earn far less than $1M and still count.

- That's the contract's definition of a usable film: 2000–2023, budget ≥ $1M, worldwide revenue > 0, from TMDB, The Numbers or Wikidata.
- So many usable films earned less than $1M. For example, 380 earned under $100,000, and 35 under $1,000 (those are likely junk entries, already flagged for cleaning).

## User  (2026-11-24T04:15:09.698Z)

Why?

## Claude  (2026-11-24T04:15:15.846Z)

Because budget is known before the film is made, and revenue is the thing we're predicting.

- **Budget ≥ $1M sets the scope.** The screen is for real financing decisions, and micro-budget films are a different business with unreliable data. Budget is known before production, so filtering on it is fair.
- **Revenue has no floor because it's the outcome.** A rule like "revenue ≥ $1M" would remove the films that flopped hardest, which are exactly the money-losers we're trying to catch. The model would learn from a world where big flops don't exist. That's selecting on the outcome.
- **Revenue > 0 is only there because 0 means "unknown."** TMDB writes 0 when it has no box office figure, not when a film earned nothing. Dropping those rows removes films with no label. It doesn't remove bad performers.

The catch is that some tiny revenues are junk, like *Aquajots*: $100M budget, $1 revenue. Those get fixed in cleaning, case by case, not with a blanket floor.

## Claude  (2026-11-24T04:16:54.498Z)

Fair challenge. Successes like *Paranormal Activity* and *Napoleon Dynamite* do exist. The data is the problem, not the idea:

| Budget | Films | Have revenue | Loser rate (if revenue known) |
|---|---|---|---|
| < $1K | 12,214 | 14% | 72% |
| $1K–100K | 13,287 | **7%** | 64% |
| $100K–1M | 4,984 | **19%** | 64% |
| $1–5M | 4,190 | 40% | 70% |
| $20M+ | 2,850 | 91% | 63% |

- **Budgets under $1K are mostly junk.** These are typos and placeholders, like "5" meaning $5M.
- **Revenue is mostly missing under $1M.** Only 7–19% of those films have a box office figure. The ones that do are mostly films that got a theatrical release and someone reported the numbers, so they aren't a fair sample. The S4 missing-revenue problem we already have would get much worse.
- **It's a different business.** Micro-budget films mostly make money from festival sales and streaming deals, not box office, so "revenue ≥ 2.5× budget" doesn't describe success the same way.

**Can it change?** Yes, but the $1M floor is in the frozen contract. Changing it needs a dated amendment that you and Matt both agree to.

If you're curious, a middle option is a sensitivity check: run the final model once with a lower floor, like $100K, and see whether results hold. That answers your question without changing the main population.

````
# A10 Project Purpose Contract — FROZEN 2026-11-17

Date drafted: 2026-11-17. Analyst: Matt Sorensen. AI role: Problem Setter, then Challenger (Claude Code, decision-statement-builder skill).
Source candidate: #1 in `report/A10_problem_scan_2026-11-17.md`.
Status: **FROZEN 2026-11-17, approved by Matt Sorensen.** This was done before any analysis of how inputs relate to the outcome; only structural profiling and join tests have been run. Any later change requires a dated amendment, added below, with a stated reason.

## Contract fields

| Field | Contract answer |
|---|---|
| **Purpose pathway** | **Predictive** (the one primary path). An explanatory layer reports how much director track record adds to the prediction. That's association only, with no causal claim. |
| **Decision** | At the financing stage, before production, the acquisitions team decides for each incoming project whether to **flag for deep review**, **proceed on standard review**, or **pass**. |
| **Action** | Each year, the 20% of projects with the highest predicted risk go to deep review (comparable-film analysis, a second reader, renegotiating terms). The rest get standard review. The screen never rejects a project on its own. |
| **Decision time** | When the financing decision is made, before production. **Allowed inputs:** budget, genre, director's track record from earlier films only, production companies' track record from earlier films only, planned runtime, planned release month and quarter, original language, production country. **Prohibited inputs (known only after release):** revenue, box office, vote counts and averages, popularity, critic and audience scores, review text, TMDB keywords (crowd-edited after release). |
| **Population & unit** | Unit = **one feature film at its financing decision.** Population = feature films released 2000–2023 with a reported budget ≥ $1M and reported worldwide revenue > 0, excluding adult titles. Training: 2000–2015. Test: 2016–2019. Stress test: 2020–2023 (COVID era), reported separately. |
| **Outcome / target & horizon** | Positive class = **"money-loser": worldwide revenue < 2.5 × budget.** The 2.5× multiple is a labeled assumption (a commonly cited rule of thumb for covering marketing and the exhibitor's share). It's rerun at 1×, 2× and 3× as a sensitivity check. Horizon = full theatrical run as recorded in TMDB. The model estimates each project's probability of being a money-loser. |
| **Baseline** | (a) **Random 20% flagging**, which catches losers at the base rate (the floor). (b) **A simple rule:** flag projects in the genre × budget-tier groups with the highest historical loss rate, using training years only. The model has to beat (b), not just (a). |
| **Evidence standard** | On the 2016–2019 test films, the share of all money-losers that fall inside the flagged top 20% (capture rate). The model must beat rule (b) by **≥ 5 percentage points**, with a bootstrap 95% CI that excludes 0. Also report precision at 20%, calibration, and the result for the 2020–2023 stress set. *Bar confirmed by Matt at the freeze.* |
| **Value** | More money-losers reach deep review without adding review workload: same 20% capacity, better targeting. Value per year = (extra losers caught × loss avoided per caught loser × share of flagged deals actually changed) − (good films wrongly flagged × cost of a wrongly flagged deal). Each term is a **blank the owner fills in**; the report shows break-even values, not invented dollars. |
| **Constraints** | Review capacity: 20% of projects. Data rights: Kaggle public datasets, license recorded in the Data Receipt. Timing: frozen analysis by Nov 25, due Dec 4. No individual-level sensitive data, but director names are personal names, so results are reported at the aggregate or feature level, not as rankings of named people. Simplest adequate method: logistic regression first. |
| **Owner** | **Head of Acquisitions** at a representative film co-financier. This is a stand-in role: there are no real stakeholder interviews, and the report states that limitation. The owner is accountable for using the screen, monitoring it, and stopping it. |

## Rival framing
**#2, director premium:** the greenlight committee decides whether to pay extra for a director with a strong track record. It uses the same data and time but asks a different question: what one input is worth, not sorting projects. It's the fallback if #1 fails the red-team or stop condition S1.

## Prohibited uses
The screen must never quietly become:
1. **A tool for hiring or blacklisting people.** It must not rank, score or exclude individual directors or other talent, or feed into pay negotiations.
2. **An automatic reject.** A flag only sends a project to deep review, and a person makes the final call.
3. **A causal claim.** "Directors with strong track records *cause* profit" isn't supported. Track record is a predictive input and nothing more.
4. **A screen applied outside its population.** It doesn't cover micro-budget films (< $1M), streaming-only releases, or films without a theatrical revenue record.

## Minimum evidence to move forward, and stop conditions
**Move to a pilot** (run alongside human review for one slate, with no decisions changed) only if S1 passes, calibration is acceptable on the test films, and capture on the 2020–2023 stress set doesn't fall below the rule baseline.

| # | Stop trigger (observable) | Disposition |
|---|---|---|
| S1 | The model doesn't beat rule (b) by ≥ 5 pts of capture on 2016–2019 with a CI that excludes 0 | **Satisfice:** recommend the simple rule |
| S2 | Removing director track record changes capture by < 2 pts | Drop the director claim and report it as a null finding |
| S3 | The hand-check of 50 joined pairs shows > 10% wrong matches | Drop the RT join and use production-company track record as the focal factor |
| S4 | Films with a budget but no reported revenue are a large share of the population, and the cross-check with RT box office shows they skew toward losers | Restrict the claim to films with reported revenue, or **redirect** |

## Red-team (Challenger)

**Weakest link 1: a filter I set earlier selected on the outcome. *This is an AI correction.*** The "usable films" filter I used in the join tests required **≥ 50 TMDB votes**. Vote count is measured after release and rises with success (Spearman 0.48 with log ROI). Filtering on it silently drops obscure flops, which are exactly the films the screen exists to catch. That would make the loss rate look lower and the model look better than it is. **Fix:** the population now uses budget ≥ $1M and revenue > 0, with no vote filter (see above). This is a strong candidate for the report's required "material AI correction."

**Weakest link 2: films with missing revenue.** 84,135 released TMDB films have a budget, but only 18,398 also have revenue. Films with no revenue on record are likely to include unreported flops. If so, the population is short on losers, and the base rate and capture will be biased. **Fix:** Phase 2 measures how many films have a budget ≥ $1M but no revenue, and uses RT domestic box office to estimate what those films earned (stop condition S4).

**Weakest link 3: is the value logic real?** Real financiers have scripts, cast packages, comparable films and presale data that a public-data screen doesn't. So could this ever beat their judgment? **Answer:** it isn't meant to replace their judgment. It's a base-rate check that decides where scarce deep-review time goes. The value claim is limited to "better targeting at the same capacity," and the report must say that we can't compare against the experts' actual track record, which isn't in the data.

**Weakest link 4: inputs that sit between "planned" and "actual."** TMDB records the *final* budget and runtime, not the planned ones, and they can drift during production, possibly more for troubled productions. That's a mild leak. **Fix:** report it as a limitation, and as a robustness check, refit using budget tiers rather than exact dollars.

**Did the dataset pick this problem?** Partly, and the scan flags it. Budget and revenue being available made this candidate feasible. The decision (where to spend limited review time) is still real and has an owner, so it stays, with the population limits stated openly.

**The course's five-question check**
1. *Predicting, changing, or describing?* Predicting: the risk of a loss at the financing stage. The director layer describes only, and nothing here claims to change outcomes.
2. *Where's the evidence and data receipt?* TMDB and the two RT files in `data/raw/`. The Data Receipt is plan step 8, still to do.
3. *What would make us stop, and would we recognize it?* S1–S4 above. Each one is a number checked against a stated threshold.
4. *Which CRISP-DM phase are we in?* Business Understanding. Only structural profiling has been done; no relationships with the outcome have been modeled.
5. *What exact quantity is being claimed?* The share of 2016–2019 money-losers (revenue < 2.5× budget) caught in the top 20% of predicted risk, compared with the genre × budget rule, with a 95% CI.

## Verification
- Every field has a specific answer: yes.
- Rival framing and prohibited uses are both present: yes.
- Stop conditions are observable triggers: yes, S1–S4.
- It has survived a real Challenger attack: four weak links were attacked, and one led to a change in the population definition.

- [x] $1M budget floor confirmed by Matt, 2026-11-17.
- [x] Instructor approval of the path: not required for this project (confirmed by Matt, 2026-11-17).
````

S4 is still triggered at both floors, and lowering the floor to $100K makes it much worse.

| | $1M floor (now) | $100K floor | $100K–1M films only |

\*Based on the few missing-revenue films (3–5%) that have a US box office figure. Almost all of them earned less than their budget in the US.

**What it means:**
- **Missing revenue mostly means the film flopped.** The films that report revenue are mostly the ones that did well.
- **This weakens our $100K argument.** We only see 17% of the $100K–1M films, and those are probably the winners. So the "14% made 10× their budget" figure is likely inflated by the same effect.
- Adding the $100K–1M films gives 833 more usable films, but they're a skewed sample.

**Options:**
1. **$100K floor anyway.** The contract's own fix for S4 then applies: limit every claim to "films with reported revenue."
2. **Keep $1M as the main analysis and rerun at $100K as a sensitivity check** (my recommendation). That keeps your question about cheap films in the report without basing the main result on the most skewed data.
3. **Keep $1M** and record S4 as a limitation.

## Claude  (2026-11-24T04:39:23.758Z)

I added §4 to your notebook. It covers 50 repeated columns grouped into 19 concepts, measured on the 6,838 usable films.

**Combining helps a lot**

| Concept | Best single source | All sources combined |
|---|---|---|
| Budget / revenue | 87–88% | 100% (already combined in `fin_*`) |
| MPAA rating | 64% | **76%** |
| Domestic gross | 64% | 76% (post-release, only used for checks) |

**Combining barely helps; one column already covers almost everything**

| Concept | Main column fills | Other sources add | Extra columns |
|---|---|---|---|
| Runtime | 98% | +0% | 3 columns add 1–26 films each |
| Release date | 98% | +2% | 3 columns add **0** films |
| Genre | 97% | +2% | `sl_genres` adds 0 |
| Language | 98% | +2% | |
| Country | 95% | +3% | |
| Director | 80% | +2% | |
| Writer | 78% | +3% | |
| Critic score | 76% | +3% | 2 of the 4 columns add 0 |

**Thin no matter what**
- Cast: 60%.
- Franchise: 15%.
- Source material and creative type: about 63%. Only The Numbers has them.
- Director is missing everywhere for 1,209 films (18%).

**Caveat:** the "duplicates" don't always agree.
- Release date: TMDB records the first release anywhere; the others record the US release.
- Genre: each source uses a different list of genres.

So for those two concepts, the decision is which definition to use, not just which column fills the gaps.

**Next step:** pick a rule for each concept. My default is to keep the fullest column and fill its gaps from the others in order. The extra columns move to a "source detail" group that the model doesn't use. Should I go concept by concept with you, or draft all the rules and you review them?

## Claude  (2026-11-24T13:28:27.581Z)

The draft rules are in your notebook as **§4b**: one row per concept, 18 rules (C1–C18). Nothing is applied yet.

**How they work**
- Each concept becomes one combined column, filled from the fullest source first.
- A `_src` column records which source each value came from.
- The ~50 original source columns move to a "source detail" group that the model never sees.
- Every input that isn't 100% filled gets an "unknown" flag instead of a guessed value.

**Calls I made that you may want to check**
- **MPAA rating:** I standardized it to G / PG / PG-13 / R / NC-17 / NR. One catch: RT has no "Not Rated" option, so a blank RT rating may mean the film was never rated, not that the rating is unknown.
- **Company and distributor names don't match across sources** ("Warner Bros." vs "Warner Bros. Pictures"). Other sources only fill TMDB's blanks; standardizing the names is a later cleaning step.
- **Language:** `tn_Languages` lists every language spoken in the film, not the original one, so it's left out of the combined column.

**Three questions for you**
1. **Release date:** use the US theatrical date first, with TMDB's date as the fallback? US dates cover 78% of films.
2. **Cast:** drop it as an input? It's only 5% filled for 2020–23, because that source was scraped in 2020.
3. **Audience score:** it can never be a model input, so keep it for description or drop it?

````
# emba-560-data-analytics

EMBA 560 **A10** team project: a pre-production **money-loser screen** for film financing.
Due **Fri Dec 4, 2026, 3:30 PM**.

- Frozen scope: [`A10_purpose_contract_FROZEN_2026-11-17.md`](A10_purpose_contract_FROZEN_2026-11-17.md)
- Plan, status and session handoff: [`PLAN.md`](PLAN.md)

## Setup (once per machine)

Requires Python 3.12. [`uv`](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/) is recommended, but plain `venv` + `pip` works too.

```bash
# 1. Environment
uv venv --python 3.12 .venv
uv pip install --python .venv -r requirements.txt
#   Windows without uv:  py -3.12 -m venv .venv && .venv\Scripts\pip install -r requirements.txt

# 2. Strip notebook outputs on commit (git filter config is local; each person must run this)
.venv/bin/nbstripout --install          # Windows: .venv\Scripts\nbstripout --install

# 3. Download raw data from Kaggle into data/raw/ (about 1.3 GB, gitignored)
.venv/bin/python tools/get_data.py      # Windows: .venv\Scripts\python tools\get_data.py

# 4. Build the unified dataset: run notebooks/00_build_dataset.ipynb top to bottom
#    -> data/clean/films_unified.csv and data/clean/reviews_unified.csv (gitignored)
```

Behind a TLS-inspecting proxy (e.g. Zscaler), `get_data.py` uses `truststore` so Python trusts the OS certificate store.

## Folder layout

| Folder | Contents | In git? |
|---|---|---|
| `data/raw/` | Kaggle downloads. **Read-only, never edit.** | No (too large) |
| `data/clean/` | Cleaned and derived datasets written by notebooks | Small files only |
| `notebooks/` | Analysis notebooks (outputs stripped on commit) | Yes |
| `tools/` | Helper scripts (`get_data.py`, transcript export) | Yes |
| `ai_logs/` | Unedited AI session transcripts (required in the final zip) | Yes |
| `report/` | Problem scan, contract drafts, Data Receipt, final report | Yes |

Licenses, access dates and grain are recorded in the Data Receipt (`report/`, plan step 8).

## Notebook workflow

**Rules for everyone, including AI assistants working in this repo:**

0. **Data comes from one place.** `notebooks/00_build_dataset.ipynb` merges all sources into `data/clean/films_unified.csv` (one row per film). Every other notebook starts by reading that file and never re-merges raw data. Rerun `00_build_dataset.ipynb` after pulling changes to it. It's team-owned: changes go through a PR.
1. **Personal notebooks are for exploration.** Each person works in their own `notebooks/<LastName>-A10.ipynb` (e.g. `Sorensen-A10.ipynb`, `Edwards-A10.ipynb`). Only the owner edits it.
2. **`notebooks/A10-master.ipynb` is the team's final notebook.** It's what gets submitted. Only work that is solid (verified, runs top to bottom, agreed by both members) moves into it.
3. **Promoting work to the master:** copy the finished cells from your personal notebook into the matching section of the master, make them run standalone (no dependence on the personal notebook's state), Run All, then open a PR. The other member reviews before merging.
4. **Never edit someone else's personal notebook,** and never write exploratory or half-finished work into the master.
5. **Notebook outputs are stripped on commit** (`nbstripout`). Run `nbstripout --install` once after cloning (see Setup).

## Standing rules
- `data/raw/` is never modified. All cleaning happens in notebooks and writes to `data/clean/`.
- The purpose contract is frozen. Changes need a dated amendment with a reason.
- No post-release inputs in the model (revenue, votes, popularity, scores, reviews, keywords).
- Export every AI session to `ai_logs/`.

| `README.md` | This file | Tanner / Matt |
| `FEATURE_IDEAS.md` | Running list of candidate model features with a time-order check for each. AI assistants add ideas automatically when they come up | Tanner / Matt |
````

## Claude  (2026-11-24T13:39:43.635Z)

`01_clean_dataset.ipynb` is built and runs cleanly.

**What it does**
- It reads `films_unified.csv` and writes `films_clean.csv`, with the same 45,492 films. It never drops a film.
- Each fact now has one combined column, a `_src` column showing where the value came from, and a `_missing` flag where the fact isn't always filled.
- It also writes `films_clean_columns.csv`, a dictionary of every column's role. Only `input` columns and `fin_budget` can go into a model.

| Input | Usable films missing it |
|---|---|
| Runtime, genre, language, country, companies | 0.5–4% |
| Director / writer | 18% / 19% |
| MPAA rating | 24% |
| Distributor | 30% |
| Source material / creative type | 37% |
| Franchise | 85% |

The 90 franchise names that were run together are now split, e.g. "Batman|Dark Knight Trilogy".

**How to run it is documented in three places**
- The README has a new **Run order** table: `get_data.py` → `00_build_dataset` → `01_clean_dataset` → your notebook. If a pipeline notebook changes, rerun it and every step after it.
- `CLAUDE.md` / `AGENTS.md` have the same order, so Matt's AI follows it.

**What should we do next?** My pick is to finish cleaning first.

1. **Finish cleaning in `01_clean_dataset` (recommended).** These are the known problems that change the label or the inputs:
   - **U3:** 434 films list US-only box office as their worldwide revenue. The Numbers has a better figure for 220 of them.
   - **U11:** junk entries, such as a video game and a fake *Blue Beetle* copy.
   - Small budgets under $1K, and implausible revenues like *Aquajots* earning $1.
   - Standardizing company and distributor names, so a company's track record adds up correctly.
2. **Build the input features.** Director and company track records from earlier films only, plus sequel/franchise, release month and budget tier.
3. **Plan steps 11–12.** Step 11 tests whether pre-release reviews are usable; step 12 is the readiness check, including the missing-revenue (S4) decision.

Cleaning comes first because it changes which films count as losers. Building features on uncleaned labels would mean redoing them.

````
def numeric_profile(df, cols, zero_as_missing=()):
    rows = []
    for c in cols:
        s = df[c].astype(float)
        if c in zero_as_missing:
            s = s.mask(s == 0)
        x = s.dropna()
        q1, q3 = x.quantile([0.25, 0.75])
        iqr = q3 - q1
        rows.append({
            "field": c, "n": len(x), "% missing": round(100 * s.isna().mean(), 1),

def category_profile(s, name, multi=False, names_hidden=False):
    n = s.notna().sum()
    vals = s.dropna().astype(str)
    if multi:
        vals = vals.str.split(",").explode().str.strip()
        vals = vals[vals.ne("")]
    vc = vals.value_counts()
    share = vc / n
    row = {

        "levels": len(vc),

        "top level % of rows": round(100 * share.iloc[0], 1) if len(vc) else None,

        "% of rows in a level < 5%": None if multi

def box_hist(ax_box, ax_hist, x, title, xlabel, ylabel, log=False):
    x = x.dropna().astype(float)
    if log and (x <= 0).any():
        title += f"\n({(x <= 0).sum():,} values <= 0 not shown on the log scale)"
        x = x[x > 0]
    bins = int(np.ceil(len(x) ** (1 / 3)))
    edges = np.logspace(np.log10(x.min()), np.log10(x.max()), bins + 1) if log else bins
    ax_hist.hist(x, bins=edges, color=BLUE, edgecolor="white", linewidth=0.4)
    ax_box.boxplot(x, orientation="horizontal", widths=0.6, patch_artist=True,
                   boxprops=dict(facecolor=BLUE_LIGHT, edgecolor=BLUE),
                   medianprops=dict(color=INK, linewidth=1.5),

def profile_grid(specs, ylabel, ncols=3):
    nrows = int(np.ceil(len(specs) / ncols))
    fig = plt.figure(figsize=(4.3 * ncols, 3.1 * nrows), layout="constrained")
    subfigs = np.atleast_1d(fig.subfigures(nrows, ncols)).ravel()
    for sf, (x, title, xlabel, log) in zip(subfigs, specs):
        ax_box, ax_hist = sf.subplots(2, 1, sharex=True, height_ratios=[1, 4])
        box_hist(ax_box, ax_hist, x, title, xlabel, ylabel, log)
    for sf in subfigs[len(specs):]:
        sf.set_visible(False)
    plt.show()

def count_plot(ax, vc, n_rows, title, top=10, xlabel="% of rows"):
    shares = (100 * vc / n_rows).head(top)[::-1]
    ax.barh(shares.index.astype(str).str.slice(0, 35), shares.values, color=BLUE, height=0.7)
    ax.axvline(100 * RARE_FLAG, color=INK2, ls=":", lw=1)
    for y, v in enumerate(shares.values):
        ax.text(v, y, f" {v:.1f}%", va="center", fontsize=7, color=INK2)
    ax.set_title(title + (f"  (top {top} of {len(vc):,})" if len(vc) > top else ""))
    ax.set_xlabel(xlabel)
    ax.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
````

## Claude  (2026-11-24T14:01:37.730Z)

I wrote the deep dive into your notebook as **§6**, with charts and tables for all six columns and a findings summary (6g). I also fixed both of your points:

- **IDs and other logistics:** §5 now lists only the **16** columns that could go into a model. The ids stay in the file for joins but are hidden.
- **Release dates:** `release_date` is now the only date input. Its two ingredients (`_us` and `_tmdb`) moved to source detail.

**What the six columns show**

1. **Runtime turned up junk entries.** The longest "films" are TV series and video games listed at 999 minutes (*God of War*, *The Bear*, *What If...?*). The shortest include a 1-minute Oscars clip with a "$30M" budget. These aren't feature films, so they need cleaning out. A real film's median runtime is 105 minutes.
2. **Genre is good as is.** It's 99.5% filled, with 2–3 genres per film; Drama and Comedy lead.
3. **Production companies:** two-thirds appear in only one film, and the same studio shows up under many names (several "Warner Bros. …" variants). Track records will be thin unless we standardize names or group them into major vs independent.
4. **Distributor:** 77 distributors cover 91% of the films that list one, but the names are messy ("Fox" vs "20th Century Fox"). Grouping into major / mini-major / independent looks more useful than individual names.
5. **Countries:** 65% of films include the US. A few flags (US, UK, France, India, co-production) would capture most of it; 108 separate countries is too many.
6. **Creative type** is useful, but 64% of $1–5M films are blank vs 9% of $60M+ films. It needs its missing flag. I also fixed one stray value that had a tab character in front of it.

Nothing is committed yet. The junk-entry cleanup from finding 1 is the most urgent next step, because those films change both the population and the label.

````
 ### 6g. What the six inputs show (run 2026-11-24)

1. **Runtime exposes non-films in the usable population.** 75 "films" run 180+ minutes, and the longest are TV series and video games with a runtime of 999 (*God of War*, *The Bear*, *Avatar: The Last Airbender*, *What If...?*, *Dragon Ball Z Kai*). Under 60 minutes are junk entries (*Anne Hathaway and Emily Blunt Hosting the Oscars*, 1 minute, "$30M"). These are cleaning items (extends U11): not feature films, so they don't belong in the population. Typical films: median 105 min, middle half 95–120.
2. **Genre is usable as is.** 19 genres, 99.5% filled, mostly 2–3 per film. Drama (48%) and Comedy (35%) dominate. *TV Movie* (14 films) is another sign of non-theatrical entries. *Documentary*, *Western* and *TV Movie* are under 2% each.
3. **Production companies: track records will be thin.** 8,393 companies; two-thirds appear in only one usable film, and only 382 appear in 10+. Name variants split the same studio ("Warner Bros. Pictures", "Warner Bros. Pictures Animation", "Warner Bros. Entertainment France"…). A track record needs either name standardization or a "major studio" grouping.
4. **Distributor is concentrated but messy.** 548 names, but 77 distributors with 10+ films cover 4,397 of the 4,811 films that have one. Same studio, several spellings ("Warner Bros." vs "Warner Bros. Pictures"; "Fox" vs "20th Century Fox"), and some values list two companies. 30% blank. A major / mini-major / independent grouping looks more useful than individual names.
5. **Countries: mostly US.** 65% of films include the US (42% US only, 23% US co-productions); 33% are non-US. A small set of flags (US / UK / France / India / co-production) would capture most of it; 108 countries are too many to use individually.
6. **Creative type is informative but its blanks aren't random.** 38% blank overall, but 64% for $1–5M films vs 9% for $60M+. Where filled, it tracks budget strongly (Super Hero and Kids Fiction are big-budget; Factual is small-budget). Using it needs the `creative_type_missing` flag. One stray value ("\tScience Fiction", a tab character) is fixed in `01_clean_dataset.ipynb`.
````

````
 def items(col):
    """One row per (film, value) for a comma-separated list column."""
    s = cu[col].dropna().astype(str).str.split(",").explode().str.strip()
    return s[s.ne("")]


def per_film(col):
    """How many values each film has (0 = blank)."""
    return cu[col].fillna("").astype(str).map(lambda x: len([t for t in x.split(",") if t.strip()]))


def films_per_value(col):
    """For each distinct value, how many usable films it appears in, grouped into buckets."""
    vc = items(col).value_counts()
    b = pd.cut(vc, [0, 1, 4, 9, np.inf], labels=["1 film", "2-4 films", "5-9 films", "10+ films"])
    out = pd.DataFrame({"values": b.value_counts().sort_index(),
                        "films covered": vc.groupby(b, observed=False).sum()})
    out["% of values"] = (100 * out["values"] / len(vc)).round(1)
    return out


n_u = len(cu)
print(f"{n_u:,} usable films")
````

## Claude  (2026-11-24T20:12:32.516Z)

I recorded "drop everything under 60 minutes." I tested your currency idea first, and it led somewhere slightly different.

**Currency**

The problem with converting is that we don't know which currency a budget was entered in, so there's nothing to convert from. What we can check is where two sources disagree. 3,921 usable films have a budget from both TMDB and The Numbers (or Wikidata):
- 80% agree within 10%.
- Big gaps show up in US films as much as foreign ones. Examples: *Awake* is $86M vs $8.6M, an extra zero; *The Chaser* is $120M vs $2.6M.

So the bigger problem is typos in TMDB's budgets, not currency. The build also uses TMDB's budget first when sources disagree.

**My proposal:**
1. When the two budgets differ by more than 2×, use The Numbers instead of TMDB. That fixes about 70 films with no hand checking.
2. For foreign films with only one budget source, make your scatter plot: budget vs revenue, US vs non-US. Hand-check only the few that sit far out from the rest.

**Revenue under $10K (75 films)**

Your rating idea splits them cleanly:

| Rating | Films |
|---|---|
| Real MPAA rating (R, PG-13, PG, G) | 50 |
| NR | 15 |
| Blank | 10 |

Proposal: keep the 50 rated films as real low grossers, and drop the 25 NR or blank ones.

Do you agree with both proposals?

## Claude  (2026-11-24T20:22:45.226Z)

**Units:** every money column is already in the same unit, whole US dollars. Thousands or millions only changes how the numbers are displayed, not the model. I'll show them in thousands, as you suggested.

**Foreign currency:** none of the 11 extreme budgets is confirmed to be in foreign currency. Four look wrong for some reason, and I'll drop those:
- *Chasing the Dragon*
- *A Aa*
- *Pink*
- *Burnout*

The rest are real dollar budgets for big films, like *RRR* and *Pathaan*.

**Label: use US revenue.** We have enough data for it, and it fits your goal better. After the drops so far (5,876 films):

| | Worldwide revenue | US box office |
|---|---|---|
| Filled | 100% on paper | 84% (93% of US films, 59% of foreign) |
| Hidden problem | 618 "worldwide" figures are really US-only | None found |

The foreign films without a US figure probably never opened in the US. Your question is about the US market, so they fall outside it anyway. The population becomes "films released in the US," which keeps foreign films that played here.

**One decision for you: the loser threshold.** The 2.5× rule is meant for worldwide revenue. The US box office is about half of worldwide (median 52%), so:

| A film is a loser if its US box office is below… | Share of films that are losers |
|---|---|
| 1× budget (didn't earn back its budget in the US) | 60% |
| 1.25× budget (same as 2.5× worldwide) | 67% |

Which threshold do you want? Changing the label and the population needs a contract amendment, so I'll draft it as A7 once you pick.

````
"""Download the A10 raw datasets from Kaggle into data/raw/.

Run from the repo root:  python tools/get_data.py
Files are gitignored; every collaborator runs this once on their own machine.
data/raw/ is treated as read-only after download — never edit these files.
"""
import shutil
import urllib.request
from pathlib import Path

import truststore

# Use the OS certificate store so downloads work behind TLS-inspecting proxies (e.g. Zscaler)
truststore.inject_into_ssl()

import kagglehub  # noqa: E402

RAW = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent / "data" / "raw"

# Kaggle handle -> (subfolder of data/raw, files expected). Recorded in the Data Receipt.
# stefanoleone992 gets its own subfolder: its rotten_tomatoes_movies.csv shares a
# filename with the (different) andrezaza file Matt's plan already uses.
DATASETS = {
    "asaniczka/tmdb-movies-dataset-2023-930k-movies": ("", ["TMDB_movie_dataset_v11.csv"]),
    "priyamchoksi/rotten-tomato-movie-reviews-1-44m-rows": ("", ["rotten_tomatoes_movie_reviews.csv"]),
    "andrezaza/clapper-massive-rotten-tomatoes-movies-and-reviews": ("", ["rotten_tomatoes_movies.csv"]),
    "stefanoleone992/rotten-tomatoes-movies-and-critic-reviews-dataset": (
        "stefanoleone992",
        ["rotten_tomatoes_movies.csv", "rotten_tomatoes_critic_reviews.csv"],
    ),
    # Scraped from the-numbers.com: budget, domestic/intl/worldwide gross, plus pre-release fields
    "michaelmatta0/movies-ultimate-metrics-features-and-metadata": (
        "the_numbers",
        ["Top Movies (Cleaned Data).csv"],
    ),
}

# Non-Kaggle direct downloads: (subfolder, filename) -> URL
URL_FILES = {
    # Box Office Mojo daily domestic grosses, scraped by github.com/tjwaterman99/boxofficemojo-scraper
    ("boxofficemojo", "revenues_per_day.csv.gz"):
        "https://github.com/tjwaterman99/boxofficemojo-scraper/releases/latest/download/revenues_per_day.csv.gz",
}


def main() -> None:
    RAW.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    for (subdir, name), url in URL_FILES.items():
        print(f"\n== {url}")
        dst = RAW / subdir / name
        dst.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
        if dst.exists():
            print(f"  exists, skipping: {name}")
            continue
        urllib.request.urlretrieve(url, dst)
        print(f"  downloaded {name} ({dst.stat().st_size / 1e6:,.0f} MB)")
    for handle, (subdir, wanted) in DATASETS.items():
        print(f"\n== {handle}")
        src = Path(kagglehub.dataset_download(handle))
        dest_dir = RAW / subdir
        dest_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
        for name in wanted:
            dst = dest_dir / name
            if dst.exists():
                print(f"  exists, skipping: {dst.name}")
                continue
            matches = list(src.rglob(name))
            if not matches:
                available = sorted(p.name for p in src.rglob("*") if p.is_file())
                print(f"  NOT FOUND: {name}. Files in download: {available}")
                continue
            shutil.copy2(matches[0], dst)
            print(f"  copied {name} ({dst.stat().st_size / 1e6:,.0f} MB)")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
````

## Claude  (2026-11-24T20:36:24.699Z)

The test worked for directors and writers but not for distributors. It also turned up a matching bug. I queried 200 films: 100 with blanks to test filling, and 100 complete ones to test accuracy.

| Column | Blanks filled | Agrees with our data | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| director | 12 of 12 | 96% | **Use it** |
| writer | 15 of 18 | 97% | **Use it** |
| runtime | (no blanks in sample) | 96% within 5 min | Use it for the 28 blanks |
| distributor | 12 of 18 | — | **Don't use.** It lists every distributor worldwide plus streamers (Netflix, Hulu, Italy's Eagle Pictures), not the US theatrical one. |
| source_material | 18 of 84 | — | Partial. It only says "based on X"; no entry could mean original or unknown. |
| production_companies | 0 of 3 | — | No help |
| creative_type | — | — | Doesn't exist there |

**The matching bug:** where Wikidata disagreed with us, our row was mixing two different films with the same title:
- *Barbecue* (2014): our director is from an Australian documentary, but the film is a French comedy.
- *Simon* (2004): the same kind of mix.

So the Wikidata comparison doubles as a check for bad matches in the build.

**My recommendation:**
1. Pull director, writer and runtime from Wikidata for all films. That fills about 470 blanks.
2. Flag every film where Wikidata's director disagrees with ours as a possible mismatch, for review.
3. For source material, fill only "based on a book / comic / etc." where Wikidata has it.
4. Leave distributor and creative type blank, with "was missing" flags.

Should I go ahead with the full pull?

## Claude  (2026-11-24T20:47:42.372Z)

Yes, mostly. TMDB keywords cover 90% of the blanks, and there's good news for your comic-book hypothesis.

**Test:** I grouped the source material into your categories and compared the keywords with The Numbers on 3,801 films where both exist. Overall they agree 74% of the time.

| Keywords say | The Numbers agrees | Blanks this would fill |
|---|---|---|
| Book | 89% | 59 |
| Other adaptation (TV, game, play, toy…) | 89% | 14 |
| Real life | 78% | 85 |
| Comic | 72% (and they find 93% of the real comic films) | 15 |
| Original | 72% | 596 |
| Remake | 50% | 30 |
| No keywords | — | 92 |

**For your hypothesis:** only 15 of the blanks look like comic-book films. The Numbers already covers comic films well, since they're big releases. The blanks are mostly small films.

**The weak spot is "Original."** For films with no source keyword, about 1 in 4 are actually adaptations that nobody tagged. That's 596 of the blanks.

**My proposal:**
1. Add a grouped column, `source_group`, for every film: Comic, Book, Real life, Remake, Other adaptation, Original. This also replaces The Numbers' 23 small categories.
2. Fill the blanks from the keywords.
3. Mark each filled value with where it came from, so we can rerun the model with and without the keyword guesses.

One decision: should the 596 keyword "Originals" be filled as Original, or left as unknown?

````
import json, shutil, sys
from pathlib import Path

logs = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent / "ai_logs"
hits = list((Path.home() / ".claude" / "projects").glob(f"*/{sid}.jsonl"))
if len(hits) != 1:
    sys.exit(f"Expected exactly one transcript for {sid}, found {len(hits)}: {hits}")
src = hits[0]
(logs / "raw").mkdir(exist_ok=True)
shutil.copyfile(src, logs / "raw" / f"{stem}.jsonl")


def text_of(content):
    if isinstance(content, str):
        return content
    return "\n".join(c["text"] for c in content if isinstance(c, dict) and "text" in c)


out = [f"# {title}", "",
       f"Source: Claude Code session `{sid}`; raw original at `ai_logs/raw/{stem}.jsonl`.",
       "Rendered verbatim: user messages, attached documents, Claude replies and reasoning, tool calls "
       "and tool results, in order. Internal harness records (request metadata, file snapshots) are "
       "omitted here but present in the raw file.", ""]
````

````
# 00 · Build the unified dataset

**Shared pipeline notebook (team-owned).** Run it once after `tools/get_data.py`, and again whenever this notebook or the raw data changes. Changes go through a PR.

**Outputs** (both gitignored, so each person builds their own copy):
- `data/clean/films_unified.csv`: **one row per film** with every source attached, keyed by `film_uid`. Includes per-film review summaries (`rtrev_*`, `slrev_*`).
- `data/clean/reviews_unified.csv`: **one row per critic review** (one film has many), keyed by `film_uid` (§9b).

**`film_uid`** is the stable key: `tmdb-<TMDB id>`, or `tn-<The Numbers URL slug>` for films not in TMDB. It doesn't change between rebuilds. All other notebooks start from this file instead of re-merging.

| Source | Adds | Join |
|---|---|---|
| TMDB | Base table: one row per TMDB id | — |
| The Numbers | Budget, **worldwide** gross, MPAA, source, franchise, companies | Title + year matcher (§4, hand-checked 50/50) plus a looser second pass (§4b) |
| Wikidata snapshot (committed) | Budget and box office in USD | TMDB id |
| Box Office Mojo | Domestic gross, theaters (US theatrical run) | Title + year matcher |
| RT stefanoleone992 | `actors`, `production_company` | Title + year matcher |
| RT andrezaza | Director, writer, RT box office, ratings | Matt's join rules (§7), hand-checked 0/50 wrong |

**Combined financials:** `fin_budget` / `fin_revenue` take the first available value from TMDB → The Numbers → Wikidata; `fin_*_src` records which. `usable` = 2000–2023, budget ≥ $1M, revenue > 0.

Rows not in TMDB (The Numbers only) have a **negative `id`** (not stable across rebuilds; use `film_uid`) and `in_tmdb` = False.

Column prefixes: none = TMDB, `tn_` The Numbers, `wd_` Wikidata, `bom_` Box Office Mojo, `sl_` RT stefanoleone992, `rt_` RT andrezaza, `fin_` combined.
--- 3
## 2. TMDB

All released, non-adult films (one row per id). Matching uses a wider year window (1998–2025) so films near the edges can still match; the contract window is applied after.
--- 4
t = pd.read_csv(RAW / "TMDB_movie_dataset_v11.csv", low_memory=False)
t["release_dt"] = pd.to_datetime(t["release_date"], errors="coerce")
t["year"] = t["release_dt"].dt.year
tmdb = t[t["status"].eq("Released") & ~t["adult"] & t["year"].between(1998, 2025)].drop_duplicates("id").copy()

# Sanity check: Matt's contract population is reproduced exactly
pop = tmdb[tmdb["year"].between(*YEARS) & tmdb["budget"].ge(BUDGET_FLOOR) & tmdb["revenue"].gt(0)]
assert len(pop) == 5766, len(pop)
print(f"TMDB candidates for matching: {len(tmdb):,}; contract population: {len(pop):,}")
--- 28
## 9. One row per film

The sources are joined one-to-one, but TMDB itself sometimes lists the same film twice (and junk entries repeat). Rows are merged when they are the same film by either rule:

1. **Same IMDb id** (`imdb_id`), or
2. **Same normalized title, release year within ±1, runtime within 5 minutes (or unknown on either side: TMDB uses 0 for unknown), and combined budget within 15%.** Title alone isn't enough: remakes and shorts share titles (*Trolls* 2016 at $125M vs a $30K short).

Within a group, the row with the most filled-in values is kept (TMDB rows and usable rows first), and its blanks are filled from the others. `merged_ids` lists the absorbed ids. `usable` is recomputed after merging.

Then each film gets **`film_uid`**: `tmdb-<id>`, or `tn-<The Numbers URL slug>` (e.g. `tn-Marvels-The-(2023)`).
--- 29
unified = films[films["year"].between(*YEARS) & (films["fin_budget"].notna() | films["fin_revenue"].notna())].copy()
unified = unified.reset_index(drop=True)

# Candidate pairs (row positions)
pairs = []
imdb = unified["imdb_id"].where(unified["imdb_id"].astype(str).str.startswith("tt"))
g = unified.assign(imdb=imdb).dropna(subset=["imdb"]).groupby("imdb").groups
pairs += [(ix[0], j) for ix in g.values() if len(ix) > 1 for j in ix[1:]]

k = pd.DataFrame({"pos": unified.index, "key": norm_title(unified["title"]), "year": unified["year"],
                  "rt": unified["runtime"].replace(0, np.nan), "b": unified["fin_budget"]})
k = k[k["key"].ne("")]
pp = k.merge(k, on="key", suffixes=("", "_2"))
runtime_ok = (pp["rt"] - pp["rt_2"]).abs().le(5) | pp["rt"].isna() | pp["rt_2"].isna()   # 0/missing = unknown
pp = pp[(pp["pos"] < pp["pos_2"]) & (pp["year"] - pp["year_2"]).abs().le(1) & runtime_ok
        & ((pp["b"] / pp["b_2"] - 1).abs() < 0.15)]
pairs += list(zip(pp["pos"], pp["pos_2"]))

# Group pairs (union-find)
parent = {}
def find(x):
    while parent.get(x, x) != x:
        x = parent[x]
    return x
for a, b in pairs:
    ra, rb = find(a), find(b)
    if ra != rb:
        parent[max(ra, rb)] = min(ra, rb)
groups = pd.Series({x: find(x) for x in set(np.ravel(pairs))}) if pairs else pd.Series(dtype=int)

unified["merged_ids"] = pd.NA
drop = []
filled = unified.notna().sum(axis=1)
for root, members in groups.groupby(groups).groups.items():
    rows = list(members)
    order = sorted(rows, key=lambda r: (unified.at[r, "in_tmdb"], unified.at[r, "usable"], filled[r]), reverse=True)
    keep, rest = order[0], order[1:]
    for r in rest:
        unified.loc[keep] = unified.loc[keep].combine_first(unified.loc[r])
    unified.at[keep, "merged_ids"] = ",".join(str(int(unified.at[r, "id"])) for r in rest)
    drop += rest

before_usable = unified["usable"].sum()
unified = unified.drop(index=drop).reset_index(drop=True)
unified["usable"] = (unified["year"].between(*YEARS) & unified["fin_budget"].ge(BUDGET_FLOOR)
                     & unified["fin_revenue"].gt(0))
assert unified["id"].is_unique
print(f"Merged {len(drop):,} duplicate rows into {groups.nunique() if len(groups) else 0:,} films "
      f"({len(pairs) - len(pp):,} pairs by IMDb id, {len(pp):,} by title/year/runtime/budget). "
      f"Usable: {before_usable:,} -> {unified['usable'].sum():,}")
display(unified.loc[unified["merged_ids"].notna() & unified["usable"], ["id", "title", "year", "fin_budget", "merged_ids"]])

# Stable key: TMDB id, or The Numbers URL slug for films not in TMDB (negative ids change between rebuilds)
slug = unified["tn_Movie URL"].str.extract(r"/movie/([^#?]+)")[0]
unified.insert(0, "film_uid", np.where(unified["in_tmdb"], "tmdb-" + unified["id"].astype("Int64").astype(str), "tn-" + slug))
assert unified["film_uid"].notna().all() and unified["film_uid"].is_unique

--- 33
# One row per film: 2000-2023 films with at least one budget or revenue value from any source
# (TMDB films, plus The Numbers-only films with negative ids). Fixed file name: every other
# notebook reads this instead of re-merging. Gitignored; rebuilt on every run.
assert unified["id"].is_unique
unified.to_csv(CLEAN / "films_unified.csv", index=False)
print(f"films_unified.csv: {len(unified):,} films x {unified.shape[1]} columns "
      f"({unified['usable'].sum():,} usable, {(~unified['in_tmdb']).sum():,} not in TMDB)")
````
